maintopic: CONCLUSION OF PRESENT SESSION-SITUATION IN FAR EAST

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: CONCLUSION OF PRESENT SESSION-SITUATION IN FAR EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one can now look to the hope of termination of this session, I thought I ought to make a few general remarks as to the probable date of commencement of the next session.
I know we cannot always predict the end of a session. Many circumstances arise that make it rather difficult to determine. But as it appears to be generally agreed that today we can expect to conclude this session, I should like to say this. I have been here for 18 years, and I have never seen any session in which there has been harder and more arduous application to an extremely heavy program than has been the case this session. I express the hope that unless international or national problems of major urgency require the calling together of parliament at an earlier date, the next session will not be convened before the month of January. As a matter of fact, some indication is given as to the degree of application to their duties by hon. members when it is realized that since October 14 last, parliament has been sitting for 171 days, and that for a considerable portion of that period extra hours have been the rule rather than the exception.
I believe in parliament. I believe that when parliament is sitting-and when I say this I speak for myself and, I am sure, for my colleagues-there is a feeling of strength to the government of the day, when that government has the benefit of the presence of parliament where, after all, we are all working
to the same end. In a community of council and in common dedication, parliament has its greatest strength.
I mentioned that the international situation might make necessary the calling of the next session of parliament at an earlier date. In that connection I think the house will permit me to make a reference to the present international situation which, while disquieting today, has in recent months revealed grounds for encouragement. We have had during the summer striking evidence of the extent to which international agreement is possible by negotiation under the United Nations. The prospects for progress on disarmament are, I think, better than they have ever been before. In the past month we have seen what the United Nations has been able to achieve in the Middle East toward the reduction in tension, and the general move toward the settlement of that problem. What has been achieved in that area is as yet tentative rather than final.
However, at this time there is in the Far East a situation which is most disquieting. The most alarming aspect there is that it seems difficult to envisage a satisfactory settlement of a dispute which has attained such threatening proportions. I think the world wants to be assured that nothing will be left undone to prevent any action that might result in the world sliding into disastrous consequences. Surely it is not beyond our capacity in the light of the experience in recent months in other parts of the world to find some means whereby in this dispute in the Far East the good offices of the United Nations might be invoked.
As far as Canada is concerned, I think Canadians as a whole would expect that their representatives will not fail at this time to explore every avenue for the settlement of the grave situation which today prevails, and it is in that spirit that I suggest the United Nations might have an opportunity and an appointment with responsibility in this direction.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Prime Minister that this session appears to be approaching its terminal stages. I also agree with him that it has been a hard working but an interesting one. I can certainly understand him when he says that
4704	HOUSE OF
External Affairs-Far East this has been the most interesting session he has had in his 18 years of parliamentary experience.
It is unfortunate that we are closing the session at a time when international tension in the Far East has increased, especially in view of the fact, as the Prime Minister has indicated, that during the earlier part of the summer tension in other parts of the world seemed to have decreased. It is not wise to be too optimistic when tension decreases, and it is certainly not wise to be too pessimistic at a time when tension appears to increase; but the situation which the Prime Minister has mentioned in the Far East in respect of Quemoy, Matsu and the offshore islands certainly does give cause for great anxiety.
The Prime Minister has mentioned the possibility of the good offices of the United Nations being invoked in this tense situation, a situation which he said had reached distressing proportions; indeed they are dangerous proportions. Anything that can be done, of course, in that direction should be done. We are all aware, I think, of the great success to which the Prime Minister also referred of the United Nations in its intervention in the Middle East. I confess that the action of the assembly on that occasion resulted in more constructive progress than I thought might be the case when the assembly was called together. I know we all rejoiced at its success on that occasion.
If intervention by the United Nations in the Far East in this particular situation should meet with success we would certainly also rejoice. But it is perhaps going to be a little more difficult in this case because intervention there would be intervention by the United Nations in respect of a dispute between two governments, each of which claims to be the government of China, and in that sense this is a dispute which is a civil conflict. The United Nations has recognized one side in that conflict as the government of China and not the other. That is a complicating feature of the situation.
I have had some personal experience in this connection, because I did once take part in negotiations within the United Nations as a member of the committee searching for a formula for a Korean armistice. Those negotiations took place with representatives of the Chinese communist government, and we did not recognize that government. On the other hand, when they met with us, they did not recognize us, and we had to deal with them in adjoining rooms. Another indication of the difficulty is that when a settlement was sought in Indochina it had to be done outside the United Nations, because red China was involved there.


Nevertheless, without underestimating the difficulties, I agree that if anything can be done with regard to this matter in the United Nations it should be done; perhaps it is something which the Canadian delegation to the forthcoming assembly could pursue.
The situation is dangerous because among other things such a high proportion of the army of nationalist China has now been concentrated on these two small islands. I am told that more than one-third of Chiang Kai-shek's best troops are there. That is creating a situation Where the defence of these islands is becoming more and more important to the defence of Formosa, and it is to the defence of Formosa that the United States has committed itself, not the defence of these islands. But the two things are becoming more closely intertwined.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said on behalf of the government, and, I agree with him wholeheartedly, that we are not committed in this matter. We are not committed, but we are certainly concerned, and if anything happens out there to involve the United States we will be more than concerned; we could hardly help being involved if only because of the fact that we, quite rightly, have a North American air command for defence purposes. As the Prime Minister has said, it is a dangerous and tense' situation.	,j
The right hon. gentleman also mentioned the prorogation of parliament. I should like to ask him whether in view of possible international and, indeed, domestic developments he has considered adjourning rather than proroguing at this time. This would make it easier for us to meet in the event of an emergency.

maintopic: CONCLUSION OF PRESENT SESSION-SITUATION IN FAR EAST
speechtext: The question of whether we should adjourn or prorogue is one that I think should be viewed from the standpoint of practical realities and the interpretation which would be given to any action of that kind. Were we to adjourn, the interpretation placed upon it might be other than the interpretation placed upon prorogation. If events should make it necessary the calling of parliament would not be long delayed; I think it would be possible to call parliament together just as quickly as it would be after a mere adjournment.

maintopic: CONCLUSION OF PRESENT SESSION-SITUATION IN FAR EAST
speechtext:
I am
sure everyone has listened with great interest to the Prime Minister's statement with respect to this session which is about to conclude and with respect to the possibilities for next session, but I am sure the portion of his statement to which we paid even closer attention was his reference to the international situation, because without doubt there

is great public concern regarding this developing situation with respect to Formosa and the adjacent islands.
We were very interested to hear the Prime Minister say that our representatives at the United Nations will not fail to explore every avenue in dealing with this situation, and his reference to the possibility of invoking the good offices of the United Nations. I think that is very interesting, particularly in view of the forthcoming meeting of the general assembly. The Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition referred to the successful action of the United Nations in dealing with the difficult and tense Middle East situation, and on that account I just want to ask one question before closing.
Is the government of Canada prepared to give leadership to the world in an effort to prevent further unfortunate developments in this crisis by proposing that the whole question be referred to the general assembly of the United Nations for action soon and, in so doing, earn the gratitude of all mankind?

I thank him for his suggestion, and also for having underscored the necessity of steps being taken to bring about a solution of the situation the seriousness of which the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. gentleman have not exaggerated in their descriptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: DISPOSITION OF BILL C-32
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement in regard to the government's intentions in connection with Bill No. C-32, item No. 3 on the order paper. On December 21 last, during the session of parliament that was then in progress, I introduced Bill No. 241, an act to amend the Criminal Code dealing with the slaughtering of animals. At that time I referred to the growing demand for action that would compel all slaughterers of food animals to adopt humane methods of killing, and indicated that it was the view of the government that some action in this field was desirable.
At the time the bill was introduced I pointed out that there were a number of considerations that had to be borne in mind and
Business of the House
a number of difficulties to be overcome before we could be sure we had satisfactory legislation. For this reason we said we would only give the bill first reading at that time, and then leave it to stand over to this session so that all those interested could consider the draft legislation and make their representations or suggestions in connection therewith.
I was particularly concerned, of course, to have the comments of the provincial attorneys general, since the provinces are responsible for the enforcement of the Criminal Code. We received comments from six of the provinces, all of which contained some criticism or suggestion which we did our best to meet in redrafting the measure. We also received comments from one or two of the humane societies and the council of meat packers, but apart from these we received very few suggestions from individuals or organizations.
I accordingly introduced this session a new bill, No. C-32, which was given first reading on June 25. This bill includes modifications which were suggested by the limited number of comments we had received.
Notwithstanding our conscientious attempts to provide legislation that would meet the situation we nevertheless, since June 25, have received strong representations from a large number of sources to the effect that it is not satisfactory. I must inform the house that most of these representations received after the introduction of Bill No. C-32 this session are from persons or organizations we had not previously heard from, or alternatively they raised points not raised in the earlier submissions, and that it would have been most helpful if we could have received them subsequent to the introduction of the bill at the previous session and prior to the introduction of the new bill at this session. It was for that purpose that we had allowed it to stand over after first reading last year. However, the fact is that we did not receive them until after we had introduced Bill No. C-32, and the result is that we are now faced with a number of conflicting representations and points of view, many of them involving new considerations of real substance which frankly it has not been possible to reconcile or resolve in the time at our disposal since they were received.
The submissions which raise new considerations deal with such points as the problem of providing for those cases where slaughter, or preparation for slaughter, is carried out in conformity with certain religious ritual; the designation of approved appliances; the availability in Canada of equipment necessary particularly in the case of certain classes of animals; the desirability of defining

Business of the House
"humane method" in advance so those installing certain devices will know for certain that the expenditures made will not be thrown away; the problem of legislating in such a way that large commercial slaughterhouses will be covered without at the same time imposing conditions which it is impracticable or impossible for small concerns or individual farmers to comply with, all matters which present real problems when criminal legislation is concerned.
Strong representations on one or all of these matters have been received from religious organizations, from humane slaughter societies, from small packers, from large packers and from individual farmers and farm organizations, representations of a nature and from sources which are entitled to careful consideration. Unfortunately, as I say, they were received after Bill No. C-32 was introduced.
In the face of these comments and objections I have come reluctantly to the conclusion that it is not possible at this time to find a legislative formula that would resolve all the difficulties that are involved. I wish to assure the house that we in the Department of Justice have tried conscientiously to find such a formula, and express my regret that we have been unable to do so. Accordingly I have come to the conclusion that it would not be in the public interest to proceed with Bill No. C-32 at this session.
We are still convinced, however, that it is desirable that some action be taken. It is our present feeling that the best way to proceed would be to place the matter before a committee of parliament in order that evidence and opinions of all those concerned may be heard and studied, in the expectation that in this way and with the assistance of members of parliament themselves we may work out a satisfactory method of meeting the problem. Accordingly it is our intention to introduce a further draft proposal at the next session which will be placed before the appropriate committee of the house, or possibly of both houses, for their study and consideration.
It is my hope that in the meantime all concerned will give the matter further consideration and prepare their submissions, so that at an early date next session the committee may proceed with its study and hear evidence which should be helpful in enabling parliament to determine the best course to follow in bringing about a solution.
I cannot conclude, Mr. Speaker, without expressing my appreciation for the co-operation I have received from interested organizations. I should also add that it is a matter of great satisfaction to me that a number of

the large meat processing plants have already installed humane devices for the slaughter of food animals.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, the minister's
statement deals with a matter which we had anticipated would have been brought before the house this session. Indeed, the minister himself indicated that; but in the circumstances I do not think anyone can object to the stand he has taken and the course he proposes. I think the course he has suggested, namely that the subject should be referred to a committee at the next session of the house, is a good one.

speechtext:
I want to draw the minister's attention to the text of the communique issued at the conclusion of the federal-provincial conference on November 26, and particularly to the last two paragraphs in that communique, which read as follows:
Possible changes in the tax-sharing arrangements act were discussed but it was understood that no endeavour would be made to reach conclusions on this matter prior to further consideration of the subject by the dominion government in the light of the public statements made by the provincial representatives in open sessions and the discussions which took place in committee.
All delegations wish to express their pleasure at the opportunity which the conference afforded to put their views before the others who were present. It was agreed that a subsequent meeting be held as soon as possible in the new year in accordance with the proposal made by the dominion government in calling this conference.

Well, as I look at the calendar on the table I find that this is September 6. This conference has neither met nor have we been able, despite repeated requests throughout the session, to get any indication as to when the conference might be called or indeed if the conference will be called at all. All hon. members are aware of the fact that one Saturday morning in January last the minister came into the house and read the text of a telegram he had sent to the premiers of the ten provinces indicating that the federal government in its wisdom, as a unilateral act, was going to make a change in the taxsharing arrangement to increase the base on which the share of the income tax of the provinces was calculated from 10 per cent to 13 per cent. We all remember that the minister had some difficulty with his arithmetic, and he spent most of the next week correcting it, but that is a minor matter.
The major matter is that the preceding parliament had passed an act, valid for one year only, an act which applies to the fiscal year in which we are now, and an act which will expire not long after the opening of the next session if it comes, as the Prime Minister in his prognostication suggested it would, some time in January.
I said this in the budget debate, and I would remind the minister that no reply was given at that time. I said I felt that it was a deliberate design of the government to have it happen this way, so that next January the provinces would be faced with another take it or leave it, unilateral proposition. That appears to be what is in contemplation.
There is, of course, an alternative which would be even less acceptable, I should think, to the provincial governments, namely that the government should just allow the legislation to lapse and go back to the previous arrangement. It may be that, in view of the staggering proportions of the minister's deficit, that is his secret intention. However, I am not seeking to speak the minister's mind; I am only seeking to speak my own.
It seems to me that this is a strange way to proceed, that it is a strange way to treat the provinces after this undertaking that the conference would be convened as early as possible, or as soon as possible in the new year. I know if that communique had been issued by the present Prime Minister's predecessor or by the predecessor of the Minister of Finance that conference would have been held long ago. The plain meaning of those words was that it would be early in the new year and I could look up statements in the proceedings which
Supply-Finance
would confirm that impression. But for some reason or another, despite what all the provincial governments undoubtedly believed was an undertaking that this conference would be held, there has been no conference and no hint of a conference from the federal government.
We have had, of course, several statements attributed to the premier of Ontario that the conference would be held at this date or at that date, but it seems evident that the premier of Ontario is perhaps not as much in the confidence of the present administration as he may have been when this conference was held a year ago, or as he may have been even as late as January, or as his officials may have been at that time. But what we know, and all we know-because we have been kept completely in the dark about this matter and there are very few places where it is possible under the rules to debate it, and this happens to be one of them-about this extremely important matter is what we have read. The minister from Newfoundland had this to say on May 4, 1947, as reported in the St. John's News. I just happened to have his comment here; I could just as well have quoted any other minister.

speechtext: Did the hon. member say 1947?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should have said 1957; I thank the hon. gentleman for the correction. This statement is in direct quotation marks. It was a statement made by the hon. gentleman at St. Stephen, New Brunswick. No, I am mistaken; it was a statement made by the Prime Minister at St. Stephen, New Brunswick. The hon. member for St. John's West was asked for a comment, and this is what he said:
-our party if returned to power will give the Atlantic provinces and the municipalities a better deal than they have now.
So far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned the minister's party has carried out that undertaking, and I have always given them credit for that fact. But what I am drawing attention to is the statement of the Prime Minister and what the minister said. The minister went on to say this, and I may say that I just picked this report up; I happened to have it here, but I could find this same statement from half a dozen other ministers, including the Minister of Finance. The minister went on to say:
"The federal government during the past eight years has been in a position where the revenue collected by them leaves no room for the provinces or the municipalities to finance the improvements and maintenance of necessary public services.
"They will continue to suffer from shortage of schools, electrification and good roads-

Supply-Finance
And these are the words I wish to emphasize.
-unless there Is a redistribution of the taxation powers. This our party hopes to bring about.
That was the policy. It was the policy enunciated by Mr. Drew when he was the hon. gentleman's leader, when he sat over here on this side of the house in another parliament. It was the policy enunciated by the present Prime Minister. It was the policy repeated ad nauseam by the Minister of Finance when he sat over here on this side of the house. I refer to the policy that there was to be a redistribution of these tax sources. Where is it? When is it going to happen, or what is going to happen?
I do not think anybody believes that this particular feature of Tory policy is ever going to be translated into action. When the minister made that confession last January that he had to follow Mr. Harris's policy and that all that he could do was pay a small dividend on Mr. Harris's policy, I believe that was the real and practical turning point.
I must say that I commend the government for their wisdom and good sense in adopting Mr. Harris's policy, because it was a sound policy and theirs was never a sound policy, but the fact is that they only did it in this unilateral fashion. They only did it for one year. No provincial government now knows, nor does this parliament, what is going to happen at the end of the year. Before very long I think the minister should come clean and tell us what the policy of the federal government is with respect to this tax-sharing problem, and particularly with respect to the statute which is going to expire this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The house has been given from time to time all the information that is available on this subject. The important measures that were passed by parliament last January for fiscal assistance to the provinces have been an important contribution to strengthening the fiscal position of the provinces and the municipalities during this year. The Atlantic adjustment grants providing $100 million payable at the rate of $25 million per annum over the next four years commenced on April 1. Each of the four Atlantic provinces is receiving benefits from that source, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland at the rate of $7J million per annum and Prince Edward Island at the rate of $2J million per annum.
The other measure of fiscal aid to the province approved by parliament in January on the motion of the government was the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the provincial share of the yield from the
[Mr. Pickersglll.l
personal income tax. That has been of assistance to all of the provinces. That is the position. The provision for the increase to the provinces from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the yield from the personal income tax was provided by parliament for one year.
The reasons for inability to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference at the beginning of the year were stated at that time and were discussed fully in this house. I am sure there is no advantage in repeating now what was said then. The government is well aware that the provision by way of increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent applies only to the present year. Whatever measures are proposed by the government in relation to calling a conference on this subject of fiscal relations between the dominion and the provinces will be announced in due course. I have nothing I can usefully add on that subject today.
The hon. member has spoken of the budget. I think I should recall in that respect that the budget deficit estimated when I spoke in the budget debate on June 17 was $648 million. In the discussion of amendments to the Excise Tax Act, when we increased exemptions from the sales tax on fuel oil when used in logging, lumbering and mining operations involving further decreases in taxation of an estimated $2 million, I stated at that time that they would increase the deficit by that amount to $650 million. The sums included in the further supplementary estimates which have been tabled, which have been discussed in part and which will be further discussed today, involve further increases in expenditures. My estimate at this time of the deficit in the light of these increased commitments, is of the order of $700 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have one or two questions. Of course the minister did not answer the most important question I asked, and I repeat it. Is it the intention of the government to allow this legislation to lapse without putting anything in its place, or is it the intention to continue the 13 per cent? That is not an academic question. We are in the month of September and every provincial government, like the federal government, has to have some basis upon which to plan its finances. I should think after the 15 months or so during which the minister has been in office he would realize that for a provincial government that is an increasingly difficult problem; and to leave the provinces in doubt as to whether this additional 3 per cent is going to be continued or whether something is going to be put in its place does not seem to me the fair way of dealing with the provinces, by agreement, about which we used to hear so much when we were on the other side of the house and the hon. gentleman was over here.

This 3 per cent was given not after consultation with the provinces, but it was simply a decision of the federal government, a decision they made and which they could unmake. I should not say unmake because they made it for only one year, but if it is not made again the provinces go back to the 10 per cent. I think surely that, at least, should be cleared up, and surely the minister could tell us whether it is the intention, before new legislation is introduced, to have a conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have dealt with
that question. I said that when it is appropriate for the announcement to be made it will be made. I have indicated that these considerations as to the position of the provinces are in the mind of the government. We showed that in January, when in the face of urgent requests from the provinces we moved to ask parliament to increase the fiscal payments to the provinces without waiting for the time when it would be possible to reconvene the conference. We have not overlooked and do not intend to overlook the need which the provinces will have to know what they are going to receive in the next fiscal year so the provincial treasurers may plan their budgets accordingly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What the minister is
saying is that in his own good time and out of his own superior wisdom he will condescendingly let the provincial treasuries know whether he is going to give them anything and, if so, what it is going to be; and that in the meantime this House of Commons, from which he is craving supply at this moment, has no right to know anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not what
the minister said at all. That is not the spirit in which the minister spoke at all. The minister I think indicated an understanding attitude toward the problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will leave it at that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This further item of departmental administration makes it possible for me to return to a matter which I raised the other day in connection with the conversion loan. I shall do so very briefly in order to make sure that the record is straight and that there is no misunderstanding concerning the matter.
The other day I asked the minister a question. I did not make a statement, I asked him a question as to what were the additional interest charges the taxpayers will have to pay, and I went on to mention charges which had been estimated to be as high as $100 million per year for the next 25 years. Then in order to make it quite
Supply-Finance
clear that this was an estimate made by someone else I said that, of course, the amount would depend on how successful the operation will be. We learned last Tuesday, that $5 billion had been reconverted and most of it, I suppose, would be into the 25-year bonds.
During the luncheon recess on the day of that debate the minister got his own figures from the Bank of Canada. He brought them into committee in the afternoon. On the basis of those figures he challenged my mathematics. I must say I thought he was brave in bringing up our comparable ability at mathematics. Mine is certainly not great, as he indicated, but his own record speaks for itself. He and his supporters got a good deal of pleasure from the discrepancy between the figure I reported as having been estimated by a certain source at $100 million and his Bank of Canada figure of $49 million. I do not begrudge the minister his moment if not of truth, at least of amusement over this comparison, but I have had an opportunity to look into the matter a little further and I think it should now be cleared up.
If the figure of $6.4 billion is taken-that is the objective of the loan and it is undoubtedly on that basis that the estimate I gave to the minister was made-and if the calculation is made on the basis of the success of the loan and the conversion into 25-year bonds where the interest rate is 1J per cent greater, the amount-and I am sure the minister's mathematics will agree with mine here-of extra interest charged to the taxpayer will be $96 million. So this particular estimate made on that basis of calculation was $4 million out; it should be $96 million instead of $100 million.
The minister gave his figure of $49 million, but he did not explain it or justify it. I suppose he explained it to this extent; he said that the amount was based on the $5 billion converted to date, which is a very different basis of calculation from the one taken in the calculation I gave. He gave the impression that our calculations were made on the same basis, which was not valid.
Assuming that all the bonds in the amount mentioned by the minister, that is to say $5 billion, have been converted-all of them- into 25-year bonds, the additional interest charge which would have to be paid on the basis of calculation he used would be $75 million. That is, assuming there was a 100 per cent conversion from the victory bonds to the 25-year bonds in the amount of $5 billion, the additional annual interest charge would be $75 million and not $49 million. Therefore if the minister's figure, given to him as he states by the Bank of Canada, of $49 million is accurate, then the government

Supply-Finance
has failed to reach its major objective, which was to convert the old bonds into the new 25-year bonds, by that amount.
The difference, therefore, was not due to any error in arithmetic on my part but to the calculation which the minister made on a basis which brings about a figure of $49 million only. But this does have serious implications because I suggest it means that not as high a proportion of these bonds in the $5 billion total is being converted to the 25-year bonds as is desirable.
Before I sit down I would like to ask the minister another question on this point. Is he in a position to say whether the new conversion bonds will be supported at par, or will their value be allowed to fluctuate and find its own level on the market? That, as the committee knows, is an important question which is of great interest to bondholders and also to this committee, because the answer the minister gives will throw some light upon the monetary policies which will be applied in our country in the future, and in the very near future, when some monetary questions will have to be decided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for the information he has given but I certainly intend to correct the statement, which he repeated, that my figure was a miscalculation. It was no miscalculation at all. Why do I have to read again what I said? I said: "I want to ask the minister what are the additional interest charges the taxpayers will have to pay, which have been estimated to be as high as $100 million." That estimate has appeared in the press and that is where I read it; in a reputable journal too, and it was not the Winnipeg Free Press.
Then I went on to say, being particularly cautious, that the final figure would depend, of course, on the amount of bonds converted and into what maturity they were converted. Then the minister came back with his figure of $49 million without any explanation at all. He has given us his explanation this morning, and it is an important explanation.

Indeed, it does explain where he gets his figure of $49 million. The figure of $100 million was obviously based on the assumption that the operation would be completely successful and that the conversion would be entirely into the 25-year bonds.
I am sure it was the desire of the government to get as high a proportion of this conversion into the long term bonds as possible. I am sure that was the desire in order to make it easier for future financing. What we have learned this morning is of importance; that of the $5 billion converted, $1.8 billion has gone into the 25-year bonds and smaller amounts into the earlier maturities. Therefore, the calculation made on that basis does come to this figure of $49 million. To that extent it is true that the burden on the taxpayer will be easier. But to that extent also the operation has not been as successful, I assume, as the government would have liked it to be. However, there is still another week to go, and perhaps there will be more 25-year bonds taken out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We think this has been highly successful. We did not think for one minute that every holder of victory bonds would convert into the 25-year maturity. For instance, bonds in the case of many institutions are not normally purchased for periods of 25 years; they usually operate in the shorter term market. We think the response, with 36 per cent of the conversions in terms of the amount up to Wednesday of this week going into the 25-year bond, is a highly satisfactory result. There should not be any impression, therefore, that there has been a lack of success or any disappointment over the results. The results in all respects have been most highly successful.
I shall simply make this further observation with regard to interest yield. There has been a great deal of loose talk, and some of it in this house, about an increase in interest rates of 1J per cent. From the figures I have given the committee it will be quite clear that as of the close of the market on Wednesday of this week the net increase in interest on the aggregate of conversions, far from being 1J per cent has been a fraction under one per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before this item carries I want to refer the minister to a question which I placed on the order paper on July 1, question No. 143. This question was in two parts. Part 1 reads as follows:
How many loans have been granted to persons, companies or firms in Newfoundland by the industrial development bank in each year since 1950?
Part 2 reads:
What is the amount of each loan?
Supply-Finance
On August 18 as reported in Hansard on page 3754, the minister gave the following answer:
1.	1950, 1; 1951, 1; 1952, 1; 1953, nil; 1954, 1; 1955, 1; 1956, 1; 1957, 2; 1958, 2.
2.	It is not in the public interest to disclose this information, which is a matter of customer and bank relationship.
Just because the minister makes that statement it does not automatically follow that he is right, because I do not think the minister is any less fallible than the rest of us.
It would certainly be in the public interest to know the amount of loans made by this bank in any fiscal year or in any calendar year. If it is correct that there was only one loan in each of six years in the nine-year period, that might perhaps justify what the minister said, though I would point out to him that we were not asking who got the loans and we had no interest in knowing who the customers were, but rather we wanted to know only the amounts of the loans. I do not think the minister could claim it would not be in the public interest to tell the committee what was the total amount of the loans granted in that nine-year period, and I ask him to give that information to the committee at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend may not appreciate that the industrial development bank is not an adjunct of the Department of Finance at all. The industrial development bank is a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada. It operates as an independent institution. I have no control over the industrial development bank. Some hon. members speak and act as though I had. I wish to make it clear that the industrial development bank is a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada and is responsible to the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada has a separate, independent status created by a statute of this parliament. The industrial development bank, it is true, reports from time to time as to the extent of its lending operations. Those reports appear publicly from time to time.
As to its operations in Newfoundland or in any other province, I believe that information may be available from the bank sources; but if it is, it is available to my hon. friend just as much as it is to me, because of the fact the bank operates independently of the government and independently of the Department of Finance.
When this question was asked, appearing as question No. 143 of this session, I take it the bank had a very good reason for not giving the amount, because it would have tagged each individual loan. It is not as though there had been a large number of

Supply-Finance
loans so that the answer to the second question would not have disclosed the affairs of each particular individual borrower. I think my hon. friend will appreciate that it is not quite fair to expect a bank which operates in this independent way to disclose its individual operations and transactions with its customers. It makes its reports to the Bank of Canada and gives general disclosure of its operations, but not of any individual transaction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I understand it the Bank of Canada is an instrument of federal government fiscal policy-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no. I wish to correct my hon. friend on that, Mr. Chairman. The Bank of Canada has an independent status under legislation enacted by this parliament, and it has powers that are conferred upon it directly by parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the government going to make the amendment promised by the Minister of Justice during the last campaign?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: To what amendment does my hon. friend refer?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An amendment to the Bank of Canada Act. I believe the industrial development bank could play a much more useful role than it is playing at the present time. At present all it can do is lend money to individuals for capital industrial investment. That is not the great need at this time, particularly in Newfoundland. Whether or not the industrial development bank is a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada, it has been set up to give the public a service which they cannot get from the regular chartered banks. If it is not doing that there is no justification for its existence.
At the present time I fail to see that it is doing very much more than the ordinary commercial banks are doing and in so far as Newfoundland is concerned, as the record of that question shows, it has been of very little use at all. What we want to achieve is better use of this bank, and we want to enable it to function in a way that will be of greater benefit particularly to the smaller business people in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend can complain as he wishes if he thinks the industrial development bank is making loans in fields in which it should be operating, but I would ask him before he makes such criticisms to consult the statute under which this bank operates, because this bank's powers of lending are defined and prescribed strictly by parliament. I am informed that the bank receives many applications that are completely outside the
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).1
scope of operations in which the bank is permitted by parliament to engage.
The annual report of the industrial development bank for the fiscal year 1957 is available. It shows the classification of provinces in terms of aggregate statistics. It shows that to September 30, 1957-that is to say the close of the bank's fiscal year at September 30 a year ago-the gross authorization on loans, investments and guarantees for Newfoundland was $475,000 less calculations and reductions. The gross authorizations during the fiscal year 1957 amounted to $255,000. The current authorizations at September 30, 1957, were $433,000, and the amount of loans outstanding in Newfoundland at September 30, 1957, was $315,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thank the minister, but I know that information is in the report. What the minister said confirms my complaint to the effect that the bank is restricted in its operations by an act of parliament. I believe that act should be opened and broadened so the scope of the bank's operations could be extended, particularly to meet the needs of the small businessmen in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall take only a few minutes of the time of the committee because I know the minister is very anxious to complete his estimates, and I do not blame him for that.
By the end of this month the commonwealth trade and economic conference will have taken place in Montreal; in fact the minister told us it would take place between September 15 and 26. A few days later, on October 6, another very important conference will be held in New Delhi and the Minister of Finance will attend as a representative of Canada in his capacity as Minister of Finance. I know he will have great responsibilities at both conferences. One of the most important items on the agenda at the New Delhi conference will be that of expanding the operations and functions of the international monetary fund and the world bank.
Early in the year we knew something was to be done, but of course we did not know how it was to be accomplished. There were rumours in the spring that perhaps there would be an increase in the price of gold. An interesting article on this subject appeared in the Montreal Gazette of Wednesday, June 4, 1958, one paragraph of which I wish to cite:
The possibility that the United States might so act-
-to increase the price of gold. I continue:
-was widely rumoured last week. Plenty of evidence could be marshalled to support such a

move. The most persuasive is the threat of a squeeze on. international short term credit if the American recession deepens.
Of course this threat has materialized. 1 continue:
"The simple reason for the thoroughly undesirable squeeze on liquidity is that since pre-war days, the dollar price of many commodities entering into international trade has trebled while the dollar price of gold has stood still "says The Economist, London.
That is an extract from an article which appeared in The Economist of London. Now, Mr. Chairman, we were informed in a statement by the Prime Minister in the house on July 25 that he favoured increasing the quotas of the international monetary fund and the international bank. In a very clear statement the Prime Minister outlined what he thought should be done. Of course this was not new because earlier in the month, on the occasion of the visit of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Mr. Macmillan, this was mentioned. On June 13 the Ottawa Journal had the following report of a press conference with Mr. Macmillan:
Mr. Macmillan said a commonwealth development bank "to mobilize the potential savings of the commonwealth and to direct investment" would be discussed at the Montreal conference. Commonwealth free trade and the bank were "only my hopes and dreams".
Prime Minister Macmillan addressed members of the house and the Senate in this chamber on June 13, and on June 14 the following report appeared in the Financial Post:
Macmillan's Ottawa talks concentrate on finances.
1.	Action by the international monetary fund to increase, perhaps double, the reserves of the free world.
2.	Action by the world bank to bring at least a corresponding increase in the capital available for undeveloped countries.
Again this did not tell us exactly what would happen. We were still hoping there would be an increase in the price of gold. Mr. Macmillan went across the border to visit the United States, and on June 14 the following article appeared in the New York Times:
Officials believed Mr. Macmillan's optimism reflected success in "selling" to President Eisenhower and Mr. Dulles his ideas for increasing the "liquidity" of the western world so that the challenge of Soviet exports might be met through increased trade between the western powers and the underdeveloped nations of Africa and Asia.
Following this, in fact on August 27, an article appeared in the Globe and Mail containing the following:
Today-
The reference is to July 26.
-Mr. Eisenhower instructed treasury secretary Robert Anderson to back moves at New Delhi to throw more resources behind the fund and bank.
Supply-Finance
We are told also that this will be done through increasing quotas and increasing the liquidity of the world bank and the monetary fund. However, in the same month an article appeared in the Montreal Gazette, part of which reads as follows:
This year the optimists are counting upon decisions reached at the commonwealth trade and economic conference here in mid-September to serve as a lever to pry the gold price into public debate. Once the issue is in the open, they believe, the chances for persuading American acceptance of a higher price are good.
I am not going to read the whole article, but only a few more extracts. In the article there is the following:
There is only one difficulty. However cogent, however strongly put, none of them answer the main American objection to a higher gold price. An increase would inflate American currency. Inflation, admittedly, is already present. But so far the government is still hopeful of keeping it under a measure of control. Deliberate inflation, such as would follow from a higher gold price increase, remains thoroughly undesirable. Moreover, the Americans are already convinced that the advantages of a higher price for gold-with the exception of those applying to the producers-can be pretty well supplied by expanding the functions of the international monetary fund and the world bank.
That is when we learned that this was to be done. I can understand the position of the minister when he goes to the commonwealth trade and economic conference. I can also understand the position of Britain in this matter. It will certainly be difficult to contradict the United States. I can see also why what I am about to read was added to this article:
Further, they would seem to have convinced the Canadian government of that point.
The United States would seem to have convinced the Canadian government that this was not the time for an increase in the price of gold, but that instead the functions of the international monetary fund and the world bank should be expanded by increasing quotas. The article continues:
The proponents of a higher gold price cite finance minister Fleming as their strong hope in pushing it through. Mr. Fleming may have preferred a higher price for gold but if so it hasn't been evident in his public pronouncements. Rather, the indications are that Mr. Fleming, like the Americans, favours the broader use of existing world monetary agencies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: From what paper did my hon. friend read that last quotation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
From the Montreal Gazette of August 21. I am not here to blame the minister, because I know pressure is being put on the United Kingdom and Canadian governments not to insist on an increase in the price of gold. Nevertheless I am hoping that the minister will discuss this matter at the commonwealth trade conference with other commonwealth countries. I am sure it can

Supply-Finance
be discussed. Even if the United States does not like it, it is not their conference but our conference. Therefore I hope the minister will discuss the matter. I am not saying that the minister should go to New Delhi and try to raise that point very strongly, because I think it is understood before he goes there that this question should not be brought up. In the Northern Miner of two days ago the following article appeared:
There can't be any change by Britain in the price of gold so long as it owes money to the international monetary fund. By the same token, it would be impolite to even talk about it.
That is the position the Americans are taking. However, we know that this is a very important question for the commonwealth. After all, we know that an increase in the price of gold would do much good. In the same article in the Montreal Gazette about which the minister asked me there is the following:
There is no question that a higher price for gold would have been a proper step in the pre-war world. But the world has changed. Statesmen must deal with things as they are.
We still think there should be an increase. I do not wish to take any more time of the house, but will conclude by saying that we know that the need for reserves of some kind against the vagaries of international trade and capital movements remains undisputed. Gold therefore continues to be accepted as such a reserve, and is also prized as a means for effecting final settlement between countries. This is very true because we know that the international monetary fund, for example, expresses exchange parities in gold, and also that a portion of the subscription payments to the fund must be in gold or United States dollars and that it is specified that payment must be in United States dollars of the present gold content. The possibility that reserves of gold may now be inadequate has arisen largely because inflation has increased trade values at a rate much greater than the growth of gold reserves.
Were inflation to continue it would sooner or later become inevitable that the very retention of gold for use in international settlements would depend on a rise in the price. In the event that reserves are already inadequate, an increase in the price of gold should render international trade freer, more flexible and larger in volume. A higher gold price need not lead to inflation, owing to the divorce of money from gold. We are not on the gold standard now. This need not be inflationary, either, through its effects on public finance, given prudence in domestic fiscal policy.

Even if the minister has made up his mind not to insist at New Delhi on a rise in the price of gold, I know he is anxious to do it. I know that last fall he must have been very anxious to discuss this matter. I know that the minister, when he was on this side of the house, often blamed previous finance ministers for not having insisted on a rise in the price of gold. When he was saying that he did not know for certain that these ministers had not insisted on an increase in the price of gold. In fact we are sure they did. If the minister says they have not-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not seen evidence of it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: -we are told that they did. The minister may have mentioned this subject at the meeting last fall, but if he did nothing came of it. He is going on October 6 to New Delhi, and he will have another chance. As I explained before, we can appreciate that there may be difficulties. However, I still say that this subject should be thoroughly discussed at the forthcoming commonwealth conference. If the minister feels that other finance ministers have not done their duty in regard to the monetary fund, he will have an opportunity to bring that out. When he goes to New Delhi he can ask for an increase in the price of gold, and when he comes back he can tell us that he has attained his objective.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman has indicated there have been proposals put forward, both by the Prime Minister of Canada and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, in favour of an increase in the capital of the international bank for reconstruction and development, and also in the capital available to the international monetary fund. My hon. friend is aware of the statement that was made within recent days by President Eisenhower and the secretary of the treasury of the United States, Mr. Ralph Anderson.
It is quite clear that this proposal of an increase in the capital of these two important international institutions will be discussed at the meeting at New Delhi which opens on October 6. I hope to be in attendance at the meetings of the boards of governors of both these institutions. While the subjects are bound to be discussed at those annual meetings, it does not necessarily follow that final decisions will be taken at that time. The meetings normally last about five days. It may be that the board of governors will give a general expression of its views in relation to the subject and leave the matter for further discussion and further action at the executive level.

What an increase in the capital of the institutions will mean in terms of a possible increase in the contribution of gold to the fund on the part of contributing members of either institution remains to be seen. That will be determined entirely in relation to the terms that will be established and attached to any increase in the capital, and the form that the increase will take.
My hon. friend referred to some rumour that was current not very long ago that there was to be an increase in the price of gold. All I can say is that I have no information as to the source or grounds of the rumour. I was grateful to His Honour Mr. Speaker for pointing out that I would have an opportunity to pursue the inquiry, though there is not much point in pursuing the inquiry itself, which I made to the Prime Minister this morning about his reply to an appeal made to him by unanimous vote of the house of assembly of Newfoundland, contained in a resolution which was moved by the premier and seconded by the leader of the Prime Minister's own party in Newfoundland and which was transmitted to the government, making a request that the province should be given what is its undoubted right by this parliament this session. I had not much hope the other evening when the Minister of Finance replied to the appeals to the government which were made by all the Liberal members from Newfoundland who were present in Ottawa at that time to accede to this unanimous request of the house of assembly. But the minister did not slam the door tight; that was left for the Prime Minister this morning. Despite this unanimous request; despite the fact that the leader of his own party in the house of assembly in Newfoundland had seconded this motion and that all the Conservative members had supported it, he indicated that no attention was going to be paid to the request.
This is an extremely serious matter. While there is nothing an opposition can do in the circumstances except protest, I certainly do so, and I have no doubt that my friends from Newfoundland on this side of the house will join in that protest. What is this request that the Prime Minister has turned down, and turned down for no valid reason whatsoever? It is a request made as long ago as August 11 in the first instance and made again by the assembly, as I have said, two days ago. It is a request that as an interim payment the amount recommended by the royal commission which was set up to complete the work of union should be paid and paid immediately. Why? Here are the premier's words in his original message of August 11:
I wish to stress the importance to the welfare of Newfoundland of immediate federal action on an

Supply-Finance
interim basis. The commission has clearly shown that at least the amounts recommended are urgently needed to enable the provincial government to continue existing services.
That is what we are denying or rather what the government is denying, because I certainly take no part in it and we on this side of the house have shown by our speeches the other night that we take no part in it. May I say that I appreciate the support that was given to the position taken by the Liberal members and by our leader. I refer to the support that was given by the hon. gentlemen in the corner. We have shown that we feel this action should have been taken.
What is it that is being denied or refused? It is money that is urgently needed to continue existing services, not to have any kind of improvement but to continue existing services. I want to be fair about this matter. The Prime Minister said this in his reply to the appeal and the Minister of Finance the other night put it on Hansard. I will read it from Hansard; I may say that I am reading from page 4623:
We expect prorogation of parliament within very few days and it is quite impossible to complete full consideration of the royal commission's report in the meantime.
This is the part to which I wish particularly to draw attention.
Newfoundland is receiving $7,500,000 per annum as its share of the Atlantic adjustment grant and an additional three per cent of the yield from the personal income tax this year, neither of which would have been received by the province of Newfoundland had this government not come into office. These benefits, which incidentally exceed the amounts recommended by the royal commission, should enable you to meet the fiscal conditions described in your telegram pending final decision on recommendations of royal commission.
That is the reply. I do not contest that Newfoundland is receiving the Atlantic provinces grant. I do not contest that Newfoundland, like the other provinces, is getting the extra 3 per cent. But all those other provinces are getting these things to improve their services, to ameliorate their conditions. What does the Prime Minister say to Newfoundland? He says to Newfoundland, "You can take what the other provinces-every one of them richer than Newfoundland-can use for improvements and you must use it to continue your existing services." That is what this government is saying. That is the sympathetic attitude they have taken to the unanimous request of the legislature in which their own party joined.
That is the situation; there is no way whatever of getting around it. This feeble excuse that the government did not have time to consider the recommendations of the report is no excuse whatsoever. Unless the Minister of Finance, the minister from Newfoundland
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
or the Prime Minister is going to tell us that the government is considering cutting down this award, there is no excuse. If they are considering the possibility of cutting it down, then I think they ought to be honest and frank enough to get to their feet and say so. But if they are not considering cutting it down, and if all they are considering is either keeping it as it is or increasing it, there is no ground under the sun for denying the minimum amount recommended by the commission.
No reason was given either by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance the other night. I cannot understand why the government should have taken this attitude. Knowing that they would have no debate, knowing that there would be no difficulty about getting this vote through, I cannot conceive of a reason why the government should take the attitude they have taken or why they should not have acceded immediately to this request for what is, after all, the right of the newest province of Canada. I venture to say that if Ontario or Quebec had been asking for their rights, and if the premier and leader of the opposition in the legislature of Ontario had sent a joint appeal to have something done to which they had a right under the British North America Act, there would have been no similar hesitation on the part of the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance.

I venture to suggest that if the same request had come from the premier of Quebec seconded by the leader of the opposition in that assembly there would have been no hesitation at all, if it was their right, as this is. But because it is Newfoundland this attitude is taken. I am not going to assign reasons; I am not going to impute motives. I will leave the government to explain this matter themselves.
It seems to me that more than from any other member of the government, the one from whom we ought to have that explanation is the minister who represents the province of Newfoundland in the government of Canada. The minister sat silent the other night when we on this side of the house representing the province of Newfoundland made our appeals to the government. I am not criticizing him for that. I recognize the fact that, while the matter was still under consideration, while the government had not reached a final conclusion, the minister under the doctrine of collective responsibility had no other course to follow. I found myself at times in the same position as that in which the minister found himself that evening, and I offer no criticism on that score.

But the decision has now been taken; it has now been announced. The government has said no to Newfoundland. It has said no to the unanimous request of the province. It seems to me that "no" should be explained, that we should know why this reasonable request has not been met. That is the more true, Mr. Chairman, when one thinks of the fact that the Prime Minister himself clearly recognized what the situation was at the time of the provincial conference last November. At that conference the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick both suggested that Newfoundland should not participate in the proposed Atlantic provinces grant because Newfoundland's case was a separate and different one.

I would suggest to the minister that he try to exercise a little of his influence on some of his supporters who do not seem to understand what an important question is now before the committee, particularly when we are sitting at an hour not prescribed by the house.
As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, this position was recognized clearly and explicitly by the Prime Minister at the federal-provincial conference last November. At that time the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick said or implied-in fact I think there is no doubt, but I do not want to be unfair to them and I do not want to waste time in reading that part of the record so I say "said or implied"-that Newfoundland should not participate in the Atlantic provinces grant because the Newfoundland situation was being considered by a royal commission. This is what the premier of Newfoundland had to say in reply to this contention, as reported at page 100 of the proceedings: Yesterday Premier Stanfield In his magnificent speech, and Premier Flemming in his magnificent speech, each had a paragraph of identical meaning referring to Newfoundland. You, Mr. Prime Minister, referred specifically to Newfoundland but in other terms, I am happy to say.
1 got the impression from these two friends of mine that they are under the impression that so far as this conference is concerned Newfoundland 57071-3-298J
