might as well not be here, that our ease is being taken care of by the royal commission. That is not so.
No matter what the royal commission recommends, no matter if they recommend the full amount we have asked for and if you and your colleagues recommend that amount to parliament and parliament passes it, all it will do will be to enable us, to enable the government of Newfoundland, to continue-
And I emphasize this once again.
-to continue the present levels and standards of our public services which are a quarter of a century behind the maritimes. That is all it can do at the most.
That is why I noted so carefully your words yesterday-
This is addressed to the Prime Minister.
-when you did not by any manner of means suggest that Newfoundland had no place in this conference today and yesterday. I thank you and Newfoundland thanks you for that.
Later on, as recorded lower down the page, he had a further comment-I am going to read as little as possible in order to take as little of the time of the committee as possible -to the effect that as the result of certain things into which I will not go at the moment, Newfoundland was left behind in the North American progress, and then the premier went on to say the following:
We ask the Canadian government this simple question: Do you really think, does Canada think, does the parliament of Canada really think, does the Prime Minister think, that Canada has done its duty to the new province when it implements the recommendations of the royal commission which will enable it to maintain our present levels and standards?
Is that all? Are we not to be invited to future fiscal conferences? Does that settle Newfoundland's case, just the implementing of the report of the royal commission? Are we not part of this fiscal conference when the Prime Minister said yesterday that he will recommend to parliament some additional and special consideration for the Atlantic provinces? In adopting the new term "Atlantic provinces" did he not include Newfoundland? I am sure he did. Was that not something separate and apart altogether from the royal commission? Surely the recommendations of the royal commission have nothing to do with this fiscal conference, nothing whatever.
The Prime Minister replied, as recorded at page 101, as chairman of the conference in the following words:
I will say no more at this time, but I would point out to the premier of Newfoundland that when I used the expression "the Atlantic Provinces" I anticipated what his views would be in regard to the use of that expression.
I think that clearly indicates that the Prime Minister at that time understood quite clearly that the Atlantic provinces grants were intended to be available to Newfoundland in the same way and for the same purpose as they are available to the three maritime provinces; that is, to make improvements in their services and not merely to continue the

Supply-Finance
existing situation; and that there is no connection, and should be no connection whatsoever, between the two subjects.
Then we had the telegram to the premier of Newfoundland on August 26 saying, in effect: "You got these Atlantic provinces grants which you would not have got if we had not been in office, but you cannot use them like the other Canadians can use them. You have to use them for existing services because we are not going to give you what you have a right to have," that is to say the award of this royal commission. That is what the Prime Minister is saying. He is saying, "You are a second class province; you are not entitled to your rights". That is what it is, and let there be no mistake about it whatsoever.
I am the more surprised that this decision should have been announced in the final way in which it was announced this morning, because I have looked over some of the things said in the past by the minister from Newfoundland when he sat on this side of the house. On April 23, 1951, as will be found at page 2306 of Hansard, there is one sentence which I would like to read from a long speech by the minister which in large part supports this particular sentence. He referred to term 29, and having quoted it he said:
That section gave a term of eight years within which this royal commission should be appointed. But it has been my opinion from the beginning that the financial terms have been inadequate.
The minister went on to point out that the previous government should do something about this at a time when they were supposed to be derelict in their duty in not doing it, and that is the position-I am sure he will correct me if I am wrong-which he consistently took during that parliament and which was taken also by his associate the late Gordon Higgins, who also spoke eloquently on this subject in the house. Thereafter the minister became a candidate for parliament and in 1957 was successful in being re-elected. He became a member of the government, and the representative of the province of Newfoundland in the government.
I could quote many other citations similar to this one but on May 1, 1957, the St. John's Telegram quotes the minister to the following effect:
If elected, Mr. Browne said, he would "fight personally to see that we get better terms from Ottawa (under terms of union which come up for revision this year) and to convince our party of the justice of our case". He wants to fight personally because Newfoundland's "financial future depends on how parliament treats the report of the royal commission at the next session."
That was in 1957; that was what the minister said, and it is perhaps more than anything else why he got elected. If I remember

rightly both newspapers in St. John's supported the hon. gentleman because they felt that Newfoundland needed advocates of its cause on both sides of this house. Perhaps I would not have agreed with their support of the hon. gentleman, but I agree that we do need advocates for Newfoundland on both sides of the house, and I am anxious to hear what that hon. gentleman is advocating for Newfoundland, because we have not had any evidence of that as yet.
It is not as though the minister said this before the election and then said something else afterwards, because on June 11, 1957- a day that many of us will remember, particularly on this side and perhaps on the other side of the house too, for a long time to come-the minister made a statement about his election and, again to quote from the St. John's Telegram, he is reported as follows:
Personally he was extremely happy that through Its representation in parliament, Newfoundland's interests will be protected especially in the matter of the financial compensation that we should receive and expect from the federal government.
This, therefore, is not a new matter for the hon. gentleman and I think we should be told by him why it is, and with what justification, that this course has been taken, at least with his tacit approval however much he may have fought against it in the cabinet. He has to share the collective responsibility for this slap in the face to the whole house of assembly and the whole province of Newfoundland which he and I were both elected to represent. I also think he should tell us what he is going to do about getting that consideration which was promised by the Prime Minister in reply to the question of the Leader of the Opposition on August 15, and which in large part, despite other preoccupations, could have been given between July 10 and September 6, the approximate two months during which the government had this report in its possession.
I do not rest my case there because I am willing, as I say, to give the government a year or even two years to consider the report if this interim payment is made, if the basic amount is paid, but what we do protest against is this pointblank, blunt refusal to accede to the request, the well merited request, made by the premier and the leader of the opposition of Newfoundland for what is the right of the government and people of that province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would be failing in my duty to my constituents and my province if I did not add my voice to the protest which has been raised by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, and I want to protest all the more vigorously because neither the

Prime Minister nor the Minister of Finance nor any spokesman for the government has given one single reason why this interim payment should not be made.
I want to put on record seven reasons why interim payments should be made. My first reason is that these payments have been recommended by a royal commission after a very thorough study of the economic circumstances and the needs of Newfoundland. My second reason is that this assistance is one of Newfoundland's rights, emanating as it does from term 29 of the terms of union, and was recommended as such by the commission. In the third place, Newfoundland has not received any payment which has not also been granted to other Atlantic provinces. Not a single cent has gone to Newfoundland which has not also gone to the others. However, refusal of this grant prevents Newfoundland from making full use of grants in the way the other provinces are able to make use of them.
My fourth reason is that the grants are long overdue. They are overdue by more than a year. My fifth reason is that the grants have been requested by an unanimous resolution of both parties in the Newfoundland legislature, the government as well as the Conservative opposition. That request has been made in the full knowledge of Newfoundland's needs and of the urgency of the situation, which was sufficiently great to put this matter beyond the ordinary lines of party division.
My sixth reason is that the government has itself appealed to the provincial governments to do everything possible to work out a program of public works in order to provide more employment during the winter months. The government of Newfoundland has complied with that request and developed a program of works which would create employment, particularly during the winter months, but now by its action the federal government has nullified those efforts on the part of the provincial government to comply with this government's own request.
My seventh reason is that Newfoundland is faced with the prospect of the worst winter this year that it has experienced since the hungry thirties. By granting this request for an interim payment the federal government would not be committing itself in any way; neither would the granting of an interim payment interfere with the federal government's wish to give the fullest consideration to the recommendations of the commission. However, by its refusal the federal government has decided to condemn Newfoundland to a retarded rate of progress and to condemn Newfoundlanders to unnecessary hunger, hardship and suffering.
Supply-Finance
I therefore appeal again to the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. John's West, to use his influence with his colleagues in the cabinet in order to have this decision reversed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to add my voice to the protests that have been made here this morning by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. It does seem to me that there are no grounds at all for this refusal by the present government to acknowledge the findings of the McNair royal commission and thereby give Newfoundland what we think is a final settlement of that agreement entered into in 1949.
I could agree with the Prime Minister that maybe there is good reason for taking time just now to study this report further, and I have no objection to that; but I do believe it is only fair and just that an interim payment should be made now so as to avoid the hardship that will come to Newfoundland during the coming winter.
I can see no reason why we have not heard from the hon. member for St. John's West; I do not know why he has not given us the benefit of his opinion in this instance. I believe I am speaking for all Newfoundlanders when I say we ask for nothing which is not our right, and at this time we come to the Canadian parliament asking for nothing more than justice without equivocation.
There is little need to recount the facts concerning term 29. That has already been done. There is no occasion now to comment once more on the foresight of those who included this term in the terms of union, or to restate the significance which Newfoundlanders have attached from the very beginning to this particular term of the agreement. Implementation of the recommendations of the McNair royal commission in the manner, the speed and the degree in which it is done will be a measure of the desire of the Canadian government to honour an obligation undertaken on behalf of the Canadian people.
I listened with some concern to the very definite statement made by the Prime Minister today; and while I can agree that he may require more time to study this document and give further consideration to the case, I can see no reason why an interim payment could not be made so that Newfoundland might be able to carry on over the present year at least. I was talking to an hon. member yesterday following a previous discussion in this house, and he gave me the idea that he was of the opinion that this was all a one-way street.
May I tell the committee that the union of Newfoundland with Canada was not a

Supply-Finance
one-way street. I believe the stature of Canada as a nation was enhanced when Newfoundland joined Canada in 1949. It was a section of this land, formerly a dominion in its own right, which elected by a free vote of its people to become a part of Canada and the tenth province of this federation. It is true that Newfoundland has received many social benefits and also the services of government departments which have become highly specialized over the years. These have been a great blessing to Newfoundland, but it must not be concluded that because of that fact there has not been something else going in the other direction. Over the last eight years Newfoundland has been making a substantial contribution to the Canadian economy on a commercial, financial and economic basis, and I submit that this contribution is capable of measurement because Newfoundland, unlike the other provinces of Canada, did not grow with confederation. It elected years ago to maintain its independence, and because of that fact it is now possible to measure the contribution which Newfoundland has been able to make to the Canadian economy.
It should be remembered, too, that when Newfoundland became a province of Canada it did so at a time when it was enjoying the greatest prosperity it had ever enjoyed. There was no time in the history of the province when its condition was as happy as in 1949, so the union of Newfoundland with Canada was not a device to avoid the risk of financial peril. It was a desire on the part of Newfoundland and the people there to become a part of this great nation. It is now the duty of this committee to affirm and consummate its obligation with respect to clause 29 of the terms of union agreed to in 1949. We find the present government unwilling to honour that obligation.
I say again the union of Newfoundland with Canada enhanced Canada as a nation. It added 400,000 people to the population of this country. If these people had been brought here from some European country a considerable amount of money would have been paid to bring them and establish them here as Canadian citizens. But not only did they not have to be brought and established here; they brought with them many things of benefit to Canada. They brought to Canada an addition to its area of 155,000 square miles of territory, adding a considerable area to the portion of Canada below the 60th parallel, Labrador with 112,000 square miles and Newfoundland with 43,000, approximately twice the size of Nova Scotia or approximately 80 per cent of the total combined area of the other three maritime provinces. From a military standpoint the union brought with it

control of the north Atlantic approaches to North America as well as a major protection to the security of Canada.
We have only to look at the mineral resources to see something of the further contribution Newfoundland has made to Canada. In the last few years we have heard a great deal about the iron resources of the United States, the Mesabi range, and about where iron resources will be found in the future. Those who have taken the trouble to read the report of the Paley commission of 1952 will have some idea of the need for iron ore in the United States and Canada. In 1953 Bell island alone was able to provide 40 per cent of the total Canadian production of iron ore. In that year the total production was 6.5 million tons. In 1955 this one mine alone was able to provide 45 per cent of the total iron ore production of Canada.
Oh, yes; Newfoundland has made a substantial contribution to the Canadian economy. This does not take into account the other tremendous iron ore reserves that exist in Newfoundland and Labrador. Looking at it from another point of view, when the reserves are further developed in Labrador, and when Bell island has assumed still more importance, Canada will be making a great demand on the production which will be available from these sources. The iron ore mines of Bell island produce an ore which has an extremely high silica and phosphorous content. The ore of Labrador has a comparatively low silica and phosphorous content. If we are going to develop our mines on Labrador there will be need to develop further the mines of Bell island so there may be a mixture of these two ores for the blast furnaces of Europe. One could go on and talk about copper, zinc and lead and the contribution of these resources Newfoundland is able to make to the Canadian economy, thus increasing Canada's mineral production.
It has often been said that the forest products of Canada are her very greatest resource. In Canada we produce many tons of newsprint each year. Newfoundland with a population of only 2.5 per cent of the total Canadian population has increased newsprint production in Canada by 10 per cent since union in 1949. On this island we have considerable forest resources, and the same is true of Labrador. These are adding much to the economy of Canada. I still contend that in the union of Newfoundland with Canada it was able to make a real contribution to the economy of the country.
Our fishing industry is important to Newfoundland and to Canada. In 1954 Newfoundland was able to produce 29.8 per cent of the total landings for that year, not an insignificant amount. It has been said, too, and

I believe with a great deal of merit, that any domestic market is far better than a foreign market. On the island of Newfoundland there is a domestic market of $200 million each year. Many of the things Newfoundland bought before 1949 came from other parts of the world. Today between 85 and 90 per cent of the imports of Newfoundland come from the Canadian mainland.
I believe that in consideration of the fact that the union of Newfoundland with Canada was not a one-way street in the first place, and second because what is being asked for now is only a consummation of the terms of union entered into in 1949, further consideration should have been given this request; and it could have been given on a non-partisan basis since the suggestion made to the Prime Minister was made not by the premier of Newfoundland alone but one in which he was joined by the leader of the opposition in that province.
The request that it made of this committee today is made by the people of Newfoundland. In 1949 they thought whatever agreement was entered into would be honoured by the federal government. I say again that what we are asking now is nothing more than justice without equivocation.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to
associate myself with what has been said by hon. members from Newfoundland regarding this payment to that province. I agree wholeheartedly with what has been said by those hon. gentlemen.

Thus far it seems that the request is like a voice crying in the wilderness. We are asking only that Newfoundland be treated as any other province and extended the same rights. Our joining the other nine provinces made our relationship with Canada

a two-way street of mutual benefit. I feel, therefore, that I must join in the protest of the hon. members who have spoken before me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this subject was discussed at considerable length in committee of supply two days ago. At that time the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said he was speaking in a nonpartisan tone and making an appeal to the government. On behalf of the government I responded to that appeal in, I think, a like spirit and indicated that the government viewed this as a serious matter calling for very careful consideration. At no time has there been any refusal whatever of any just claim on the part of Newfoundland.
But today the hon. member has unleashed a very bitter attack on the government, and has made some charges based apparently on the assumption that there has been some refusal on the part of the government. There has not. This report remains, in the view of the government, a report relating to a matter of very great importance to fiscal relations between Canada and Newfoundland. It is a matter that affects fiscal relations not simply today but in the years to come. It is a matter which, if it is to receive justice, must have the most careful consideration.
I placed on the record two days ago two of the telegrams which have been exchanged between the premier of Newfoundland and the Prime Minister of Canada. I drew attention to the fact that the premier of Newfoundland had publicly expressed gratitude for the position taken by the Prime Minister of Canada in this house in stating that this matter, because of its importance, should and would receive very careful study on the part of the government. In my remarks I enlarged on the fact that under the pressures of the session it simply had become impossible to give to this large question that careful consideration which it merits, and on that and the Prime Minister's statement today hon. members opposite have mounted their attack this morning.
You will not have forgotten, Mr. Chairman, that there were two factors in the situation which led the government to indicate that action by way of provision of an item in the estimates would not be possible in the dying days of the present session. The first, of course, is one I have mentioned, that the matter is a very large one and the report must receive careful and thorough study. The other, however, was one that the Prime Minister emphasized and which has received further emphasis, not mentioned by hon. members opposite, within the past twenty-four hours. That further fact is that the report has not been received with acceptance

by the government of Newfoundland. Indeed, the report has been the subject of the bitterest attacks on the part of the premier of Newfoundland.
Had this been a report whose recommendations had been accepted by the government of Newfoundland the matter might have appeared in a different light, but we are asked now to take action to fulfil for this year the full extent of the recommendations in the report while that report is still denounced by the recipient government. To proceed in the way that we have been challenged today to proceed would, I think, hardly be regarded as responsible in the light of the existing condition. I emphasize that the report has not been accepted at any time. Immediately it was made public it was received with strong expressions of dissatisfaction and critical comment in Newfoundland by the premier of that province.
If anything had been lacking in the expressions of dissatisfaction and criticism on the part of the government of Newfoundland at that time, certainly that lack has been filled since, for today's noon editions of the Ottawa papers carry reports of statements made in the Newfoundland legislature yesterday by the premier of Newfoundland. I shall read just a few extracts from the report. It is a Canadian Press dispatch from St. John's dated September 6:
Premier Smallwood says the McNair royal commission that recommended Newfoundland should receive an additional $8 million annually from the federal government "was a dead loss". "This is the first time I said it publicly", he told the legislature yesterday. "The work of the royal commission was a dead loss. And the commissioners are also a dead loss. I recommended the appointment of some of those commissioners-God forgive me."
The commission consisted of chairman Chief Justice John B. McNair of the New Brunswick supreme court. Chief Justice Sir Albert Walsh of the Newfoundland supreme court and Professor John Deutsch.
It was appointed by the last Liberal government in Ottawa to determine how much Newfoundland needs to keep public services at their present level
Provision for the commission was made in term 29 of the terms of union with Canada, signed in 1949 when a Liberal government was in Ottawa.
Premier Smallwood surprised some members by announcing, I m glad that there was a change of government in Ottawa" following the last federal election. "I was glad the minute it happened. Twenty-two years in power is too long...I don't think it s good that they got such a majority. They should have got a substantial majority but not that big.
He assured he house, "In Newfoundland I'm a Liberal. But I am a confederate before I am a Liberal. My prime interest in life is to see confederation succeed regardless of what complexion the federal government is."
Then he proceeded, as this article indicates, to attack various features of the report and some of the statements made in the report concerning conditions in Newfoundland. The

article makes mention of the fact that the opposition leader, Mr. Malcom Hollet, had said earlier that the commission might have recommended more if they had seen conditions in the White bay area. Then the article continues:
"That's the trouble", Mr. Smallwood said. "They wouldn't go. You couldn't budge them. They practically mutinied when we tried to show them pictures of our institutions."
These are but a few of the statements that could be taken from this report, and these are the words of the premier of Newfoundland delivered not months ago, not weeks ago, but only yesterday in the legislative assembly of Newfoundland. These are attacks on his part delivered against the report, and this is the report that we as a government in the dying stages of this session are expected to adopt and to ask the house to implement.
I think a great deal more consideration must be given to this situation, to the report, its recommendations and the conditions that can be given to the matter under the pressure of this particular time. We would not be doing justice to this large subject to act now in the way we have been asked to act in the face of these crushing attacks delivered against the report by the premier of Newfoundland himself. Surely it is not to be said that we are somehow in default in not moving to implement the report when the report, so far from meeting with satisfaction on the part of the government of Newfoundland, has evoked such bitter and crushing attacks by the premier of that province.
I have only this to say in conclusion, and it is a repetition of what I said on Thursday and earlier today. There has been no refusal on the part of the government to consider this matter. On the contrary, there has been the plainest undertaking on the part of the government to give this matter that careful consideration which it merits, having regard to the importance of the subject involved and the interests of Newfoundland in her fiscal relations with the federal government. That careful study will be given. That careful study which the subject warrants could not be given under the pressures of these recent days and in the dying minutes of this session.

I am amazed at the argument advanced by the Minister of Finance in explaining the refusal of the government to make this grant available to Newfoundland for this year so that Newfoundland can make up its budget on the basis of this amount, which it had every reason to expect, as an interim amount. The argument the minister used the other night, or one of the arguments he used, was to this effect. Well, Newfoundland was getting its share from the

Atlantic provinces grants for the improvement of services, and that should be enough for the maintenance of services.
At least he has not repeated that argument today, but what he has done to support his case is this. He has quoted from the current edition of the Ottawa Journal, repeating the argument that because the Newfoundland government and the opposition there are disappointed at the amount recommended by the royal commission, because they think it should be much more and because Mr. Smallwood has expressed himself so forcibly on that score, they should be given nothing at all.
The reconsideration which the Newfoundland government and the Newfoundland house of assembly want is a reconsideration upward. In other words the argument is that because you in Newfoundland asked for more as a long-term proposition, we will give you nothing now. There is no escape from that conclusion. We are not asking the government to decide on a long-term policy at this time. We are asking the government to live up to its pledge to implement that particular recommendation of the report which will make it possible for Newfoundland now to maintain its services. That is all we are asking.
Obviously they are not going to get that. The minister has said, why should we be asked to consider this matter in the dying days of this session? The fact is that in the dying days of this session they put in the supplementary estimates an item of $40 million for grain growers and one of $8i million for universities-we are not complaining about that

they were able to do that in the dying days of this session but they were not able to do this for Newfoundland in the dying days of this session. The report making this recommendation was in the hands of the government on July 10 and the session was not dying on July 10, though the government may have felt like dying at that date.
In any event that is the situation, and no amount of specious argument on the part of the minister can alter the facts. What the government says is this; because you want a loaf, we are not going to give you half a loaf. That is the situation. We will let it stand at that.

This is the item under which it is proposed by the government that the rate of $1 provided in vote 541, which has already been approved, should be struck out and the rate of $1.50 substituted therefor for aid to Canadian universities. I think I should say a brief word on this subject and in relation to some of the considerations that have been raised in this house in regard to it.
The grants to universities from federal sources were initiated in the fiscal year 1951-52. At that time the grant was less than $8 million. It was fixed at the rate of 50 cents per capita of population in Canada. That amount was raised one and a half years ago to $1 per year. Item 669 now before the committee proposes that it should be increased by a further 50 cents per capita to a total of $1.50. That will raise the appropriation this year to something over $25J million.
When this was announced in the house a few days ago the hon. member for Laurier asked me whether there had been any indication on the part of Quebec that these amounts would be accepted by that province. I gave a negative answer. The first year these grants were made available by parliament, in 1951-52, they were accepted by the universities of the province of Quebec, but not since then. In the meantime, in accordance with the provisions of the vote year by year and latterly in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the Minister of Finance and the national conference of Canadian universities, which governs the distribution of these amounts, the unclaimed portion has been accumulating. As the portion of the total grant available to the institutions of higher learning in Quebec has not been accepted by them, the amount allocated for that province has been accumulating. By the end of this fiscal year, March 31, 1959, the amount that will have accumulated for the institutions of higher learning in the province of Quebec will amount to about $15 million. The accumulation will become more rapid by reason of the increase that is now proposed.
I wish to make it clear on behalf of the government that we would wish the institutions of higher learning in Quebec to have the benefit of the provision intended on their behalf by parliament. The province of Quebec has more than a quarter of the population of Canada. Last year it had one-third of the students of all of Canada attending institutions of higher learning. Quebec pays its full share of taxes out of which this vote is made available, and the matter has been the subject of representations made by our members of parliament from Quebec.

Supply-Finance
Let me make it abundantly clear, Mr. Chairman, that this government will always scrupulously respect the terms of the Canadian constitution. It is plainly recognized that education is a field of jurisdiction exclusively assigned to the provinces under the British North America Act. As long as this government is in office there will never be any attempt made to trespass on that jurisdiction exclusively vested in the provinces.
The distribution of these sums is governed by an agreement which is referred to in the main estimates. It is an agreement that was entered into between the then minister of finance, my predecessor Mr. Harris, on March 26, 1957 and the national conference of Canadian universities, which is an incorporated body. Some change is anticipated before long in the constitution of that body, but it will not basically affect the provision for distribution of these sums through the national body that represents the Canadian universities. The agreement is in fairly general terms, but it is the document that now governs the method of distribution under the provision made by parliament year by year through the item in the estimates.
I emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that in reference to this subject of the basis of distribution this present government makes no rigid approach. We adopt no take it or leave it attitude in regard to this basis of distribution. The agreement which has been in effect now for a year and a half stipulates that the amount to be allotted to any province is determined in accordance with the population of the province. It is a straight per capita reckoning. The sum is provided on a population basis for the institutions of higher learning of any province, and is then to be distributed among those institutions in accordance with the student enrolment in courses as defined by this agreement.
Now I say, Mr. Chairman, of this agreement in relation to the attitude of the present government, that while the formula contained in the present agreement has not so far been such as to be viewed with favour in the province of Quebec, if there is any formula or modification of the present agreement which anyone cares to put forward which would permit the institutions of higher learning in the province of Quebec to participate, and which is in keeping with the national interest, we as a government are prepared to give it serious consideration.
In order to make more clear the government's position with respect to the constitutional issues that may be regarded by some as here involved, let me close by saying this.

(Translation):
The government respects and will always scrupulously respect, the constitution of this country. We recognize and we respect the provinces' absolute jurisdiction in the field of education. The increased grants proposed by the government are merely a necessary aid to universities, without government infringement upon a single provincial responsibility. As long as this government is in power, it will never encroach upon education, which is a provincial matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

Will you always respect provincial rights as did the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent?
(Text):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to take the time of the committee for a few moments, Mr. Chairman, to talk about this very important subject. I regret that it has to be done at this hour, without benefit of luncheon, but I think it is a good thing that we should be sitting right through in this way in order to complete our work. This is an important matter, and I think I should say a few words about it.
There is no doubt that in this country in the field of higher education we are approaching-I do not think the word is too strong- a crisis in the sense that there are increasing costs, increasing needs and inadequate income to meet those costs and those needs. The obligations of government in this respect are greater than ever, and this includes the obligations of the federal government in this field of higher education, always having regard to what my hon. friend has just emphasized, the paramount necessity of respecting the authority, control and jurisdiction of the provinces in the field of education.
There has never been any desire on the part of anyone on this side to interfere with that control or that jurisdiction. When these grants to universities were initiated by Mr. St. Laurent and his government in 1951, that was made quite clear. Mr. St. Laurent was scrupulous in never departing from that principle.
When my hon. friend affirms, as he has affirmed-I wish I could affirm it as eloquently in French as he did-the policy and principle of the government he is, I am sure he will admit, carrying on the policy and principle that was followed by the previous government in this field. When he says they would welcome a formula which would make it possible for Quebec to accept this kind of assistance, I can assure him that when we were in office certainly we would have welcomed any formula which would have made that possible; indeed, we certainly sought such a formula.

Now, the need is apparent and the obligation of even the federal government is apparent in connection with this matter, subject to the qualification I have made. At the present time in this country 11.3 per cent of our income is spent by all levels of government on education, and 23.1 per cent goes to defence. The needs, as I say, are increasing. The universities must expand to meet those needs, and unless financial considerations prevent it they will expand. The Gordon commission, in its report on education, estimated that in the fall of 1964 there would be an enrolment in our universities of 113,000 students. In 1955 the bureau of statistics presented a projected university and college enrolment in Canada which estimated that in a 10-year period, which would be the fall of 1964, that enrolment would reach 128,900 students. I think the figure at present is something between 80,000 and 90,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figure, when the term closed last spring, was just around 81,000, and that was a 10 per cent advance over the total of the year before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This shows the problem with which we are faced in the expansion of university education in this country. We are faced with the same problem in respect of capital requirements to take care of this expansion. An estimate has been made that for the next five years $314 million will be required to take care of this essential capital expansion, so the question arises at once, where is this money to come from?
In 1956 of the amount expended on university education in Canada, 6 per cent came from endowments, a decrease in percentage though an increase in absolute terms and 28 per cent came from fees. That is a high proportion of the expenditure compared with 11 per cent in the United Kingdom coming from fees. This is a heavy burden on student fees as compared with the United Kingdom. Provincial governments were providing 40 per cent of the cost and the federal government is now providing 15 per cent of the cost of higher education in this country. About 55 per cent is coming from governmental sources, while in the United Kingdom 70 per cent of the cost of university education comes from government. Other sources in this country provide 11 per cent.
Over the years the federal government has assisted in university education. When I was looking into this matter I was surprised to find how much had been done for higher education by the federal government, in the form of direct aid, in the form of scholarships and so on. I do not desire to detain the committee by going into it, but the direct aid has been substantial since world war II. There 57071-3-299i

has been aid to veterans and their children, vocational assistance and the officer training plan, which is a very important contribution. There have been the national research council scholarships, scholarships given by a federal agency which have been accepted I think without question by all the provinces. This has amounted to about $25 million. Then there is assistance to universities through departmental grants for research and for extension work in health, agriculture, labour, fisheries and transport.
There is, therefore, nothing new about assistance to universities by the federal government, and that assistance has been accepted in some form by all provinces.
Then we have the grants in aid about which we are talking on this particular item. As the minister pointed out, those were instituted in 1951. In 1958 these grants amounted to something over $17 million, and the minister proposes to add $8.5 million more for that purpose. We on this side most warmly and heartily support that increase. There is also the assistance given by the Canada Council of $1 million a year in scholarships. Capital assistance for construction from the Canada Council up to March 31, shared by 12 institutions, has reached the amount of $4 million. This help to universities, as the minister has said, began in 1951, and I think it is not inappropriate at this time to pay a sincere tribute to Mr. St. Laurent for his interest in this matter and for all that he did.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Nothing I could say would equal in eloquence the tribute paid to Mr. St. Laurent at the conference of Canadian universities in 1956 by the chairman of the conference, who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On that occasion in paying tribute to the wise and far-sighted leadership of Mr. St. Laurent he had this to say:
The aid that his government has extended to the Canadian universities has been given without a hint of a tendency of a suggestion of a suspicion of a trend towards a desire to undermine their academic freedom.
And he concluded as follows:
We thank you, sir, in a mood of gratitude not unalloyed by an expectation of benefits to come.
Those benefits came shortly after. They were then doubled, and today are being increased by this amount in the estimates. We certainly welcome this measure.
There is one feature I would like to call to the attention of the minister which perhaps could be improved upon. I agree that the grants should be increased, and they are now being increased. They should be increased without any strings attached to them, and that is the case here. I am sure care has

Supply-Finance
been taken to ensure that there should be no suspicion of any strings being attached by the manner in which they are being distributed through the council of Canadian universities. However, the present formula for allocating these grants, as the minister pointed out, is based on the population of each province and, within any province, those amounts are distributed in proportion to the number of students attending approved higher educational institutions.

speechtext: Yes, as defined, which makes them acceptable. Perhaps this formula could be altered as recommended by the national conference of Canadian universities, because in its present application the provinces with small populations but high proportions of university students do suffer. The grant for 1957-58 for Ontario per student-perhaps the minister could give me the exact figure, because I was not able to get it-

I had $238, but the student grant for Nova Scotia was only $148. That is of course due to the passionate desire of the young men and women in that province to have a university education, and no doubt the ease with which they qualify for such education. But perhaps the government could look into the formula recommended by the universities to see if it could be made somewhat more equitable in its distribution.
We have put forward some proposals in this field, and I just want to place them on the record, which will only take a very short time. We have proposed that the federal government should provide 2,500 Canadian scholarships and 7,500 bursaries every year to students who can pass an open examination conducted in both official languages. That would make it possible, I believe, for any young Canadian to get a university education who could qualify for it on the basis of this kind of competitive examination, and it would surely ensure that no young Canadian would be prevented from so doing because of a lack of funds.
I admit this will be an expensive scheme to put into effect. If it were put into full effect with the students studying at universities for four years it would require $25 million in assistance each year. This would be done by competitions conducted by the university association and so on. We have also proposed interest-free loans from the first university year until one year after graduation, which would constitute a revolving fund from which students could benefit, from

the interest which would begin one year after they left college. I think it would be advisable for a scheme of this kind not to be restricted to Canadians who have just left school. It also could become a most important part of our adult education.
I believe this proposal should commend itself at least to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because in concluding my remarks I refer to what he said in March, 1958. This will also show that while we welcome this item because it increases the grant, it does not implement the promises made in the election campaign by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, presumably speaking for the government. On March 4, 1958, as reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald he outlined a stepped-up program of assistance comprising the following three points: urgent increase in fellowships, bursaries and scholarships. That is something I have mentioned. Next, that federal government grants to universities be increased from $1 to $1.50 per head and that is being done, and that the distribution should be based on a national average. Finally, and this is important, a possible amendment to the federal housing act to allow financial assistance to universities for residential construction which could be repaid on a self-liquidating basis.
My hon. friend probably knows that this latter point is one of the most important problems facing the universities in their capital construction program, and if the National Housing Act could be used in this way it would be a great help to them.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs repeated these proposals in Vancouver on March 22, and on that date the press quoted him as saying also that these proposals were for 1958-59. The report goes on to say that when the minister made them on this date he was cheered by more than 1,000 students. He might well have been cheered, because he said that the grants would be $1.50 per head of population instead of $1, and that there would be $6,250,000 to finance 10,000 new scholarships, bursaries and fellowships in 1958-59, eventually increasing to $25 million for 40,000 scholarships.
These were the proposals he brought forward three weeks before the election. He also promised amendments to the National Housing Act, which I have mentioned, and as a member of a government with a great interest in higher education he put forward this program as something which would be implemented in 1958-59. This is not being done. We welcome however this increase of 50 cents in the amount of the grant, and we will be very glad indeed to support it.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks made by the leader of our party have set out this party's attitude on grants in aid to universities and the proposed increase. My hon. friend also made certain suggestions with regard to further aid.
The present formula, including this year's increase, will grant up to approximately $725 per student in some provinces. In other provinces the amount will be as low as $220 This is a most inequitable formula, particularly as it affects the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, as the hon. member for Algoma East has pointed out.
My remarks will deal with the service rendered by the small universities and their financial plight, and the group of high school students whose standards would enable them to continue their education but who are unable to do so for financial reasons. The further supplementary estimates contain an item in the amount of $8.5 million covering a 50 per cent increase in the amounts of the grants in aid, bringing the total amount paid to $25,600,000 based on the rate of $1.50 per head of population.
This increase is a most welcome and badly needed one, and meets half way the request made by the national conference of Canadian universities. This 50 per cent increase is a substantial one in the light of present revenues, and it will provide further financial assistance which will pay big dividends in the years ahead. The number of eligible Canadian universities is 91. However, seven of these are in Quebec province, which reduces the number that will receive grants this year to 84.
In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia there are 19 eligible universities as compared with 10 in the provinces of British Columbia and

Supply-Finance
Alberta and three in Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. Ontario has a total of 30. New Brunswick and Nova Scotia together have as many institutions eligible for grants in aid as have British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Newfoundland combined, despite a much smaller population. New Brunswick has more eligible universities than either British Columbia or Alberta, while Nova Scotia ranks third behind Ontario and Saskatchewan.
In April of this year the national conference of Canadian universities submitted a four-clause brief to the government. The clauses read as follows:
(1)	To double the federal grants In aid to universities of Canada.
(2)	To agree to some modification of the present formula of these grants to make the rates between one university and another more equal.
(3)	To provide financial help towards capital expenditures for departments in the physical and biological sciences.
(4)	To provide greater federal support for fundamental scientific research and for graduate studies within universities.
The request contained in clause 2 of the brief asks for a modification of the present formula toward making the rates between one university and another more equal, but apparently no action in this regard is contemplated this year. I take it from the minister's recent answer to a question I asked him on orders of the day, when he stated that no change was contemplated, that this is the case. His answer was just a "no", but I imagine that reply would not go beyond the present year and that there may be changes in the future.
In summary, the brief states that the present system shows weaknessess in that universities in some provinces receive far less per student than those in other provinces. The rates in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are among the lowest, the top rate per student being $481 and the lowest $148. The summary also states that there is failure to make any provision for the wide differences in the cost of educating students in the various disciplines. While the increase in grants rises annually in accordance with the increase in student enrolment, in 1956-57 the average grant per student was $221 and in 1957-58 it was $205, a difference amounting to $16 less per student.
The opinion has been expressed that this submission favours the larger universities. I refer, of course, to the submission of the national conference of Canadian universities. In my opinion it would be a serious mistake to increase the per student grant to large universities at the expense of the smaller institutions. Most of the larger universities are endowed and many of them receive grants
[Mr. McWilliam.l
from provincial governments; their tuition fees are higher and their large enrolments qualify them for the major portion of the grant.
On the other hand the small universities which are not endowed are continually facing critical financial problems which retard expansion and in many cases are in difficulties in meeting current expenses. The present level of federal grants in aid in many cases are the difference between carrying on and closing the doors.
In the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia where there is a proportionally large number of universities, the majority, like most Atlantic province institutions, are in the small university group. The smaller universities enrol students who in many cases cannot afford to go to a larger university. In this respect these institutions are performing a great service to Canada in providing higher education for a group who otherwise would be denied the opportunity. While the present percentage of qualified students attending universities is low, being only 7 per cent out of a possible 31 per cent, it would be much lower if small universities were not offering the opportunity. Increased grants make it possible for small universities to carry on and extend the opportunity for a larger enrolment among the group with limited financial means, which comprises practically all students in the group between the 7 per cent now attending and the 31 per cent eligible.
The government should give every consideration toward making it possible for the group who have the academic qualifications but who lack the financial aid to continue their education thus providing equality of opportunity. I wish to take this opportunity to publicly express, once again, the gratitude of the people of New Brunswick to one who has done more than any other single person in assisting young men and young women to acquire a higher education. I speak of that great benefactor, Lord Beaverbrook.
Any submission to the government to change the formula of payments should be given the most serious consideration, keeping in mind the financial plight of the small universities, and in particular the group they serve. If any change is made in the formula of payments the quota for small universities should be increased to bring about an equality of opportunity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

Mr. Chairman, just one word. I thank the Leader of the Opposition and other hon. members who speaking for themselves and their parties have commended this proposed increase represented by the present item. I believe I should make

one comment on the matter that has been raised. It has to do with the formula for division of the provincial allotment among the universities or institutions of higher learning in the provinces.
It is quite true the present formula which we have inherited from the agreement of March, 1957 and which was in effect indeed since the grants were first instituted in the fiscal year 1951-52, has created wide disparities in the amounts allotted per student by reason of the fact that the proportion of population in attendance at institutions of higher learning varies so widely from province to province. The Leader of the Opposition referred to Nova Scotia. Under the present formula Nova Scotia receives the lowest per student award. On the other hand, under the existing formula Newfoundland receives by far the highest. For the year 1957-58 the distribution ran all the way from a low of $148 per student enrolled in Nova Scotia to a high of $421 per student enrolled in Newfoundland.
This matter has been studied, and as the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi mentioned it was the subject of representations made on behalf of the governing body of the national conference of Canadian universities to the government when they met the Prime Minister and myself several months ago.
This has been a troublesome and difficult matter. No one wishes to see these wide differences. However, in seeking to bring about a greater measure of equality on a per student basis very serious difficulties are encountered because of the difference in educational forms in each of the provinces, and the difference in definitions of "institutions of higher learning" in the various provinces. It is because of the wide difference that exists attributable to differences in provincial approach that it has not yet been found possible to devise a formula which will maintain general justice as among the different provinces with a greater measure of equality in the allotment per student.
Item agreed to.

In that case I shall proceed. I am not going to raise the point of order! When the minister quite properly intervened I was beginning to read the questions I had

Supply-Finance
asked and the answers the minister gave, as found on page 4516 of Hansard for September 3. The first question was:
Were George P. LeBlanc and Alex P. Boudreau dismissed from the Cape Breton highlands national park effective June 10, 1958?
The answer given by the minister to that question was:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first question is yes.
The second question was:
How long had each of these employees been employed by the national park?
The answer to that question was as follows:
George P. LeBlanc was continuously employed from April, 1951, to the date of his dismissal. Alex P. Boudreau was originally taken on strength on October 6, 1954. Mr. Boudreau was struck off strength on February 14, 1955 and was again taken on strength on May 11, 1955. He was continuously employed from that date to the date of his dismissal.
The third question was:
What was the reason for dismissal in each case?
The answer was:
The answer to question No. 3 is that the dismissal in each case was made on the basis of a declaration by an hon. member that the employee had taken an active part in politics.
I have here, sir, a telegram which I received on September 4, the day following the minister's answer, which reads as follows:
J. W. Pickersgill, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Population of North Inverness flabbergasted at declaration Hamilton re George LeBlanc and Alex Boudreau. Five thousand people can swear these two were never active in politics apart from going out to vote. Press for immediate investigation.
Simon P. Boudreau.
I also have a copy of a letter sent to the hon. member for Laurier purporting to have been addressed-I must not say anything I cannot prove-to the minister on June 16, 1958 from Cheticamp, Inverness county, Nova Scotia. It reads as follows:
Hon. Alvin S. Hamilton,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Honourable and dear sir:
We were somewhat surprised at your recent statement in the House of Commons to the effect that no employee of the federal government had been dismissed for reasons of political affiliation.
We, the undersigned, George P. LeBlanc and Alex P. Boudreau, have been employed as carpenters by the department of northern affairs in the Cape Breton highlands national park for seven years and three years respectively. Our work has always been highly satisfactory as can be ascertained by contacting Mr. Atkinson, the recently transferred park superintendent.
On June 10 we were notified that our services would no longer be required. Upon being asked

the reason for our dismissal the new park superintendent, Mr. Brown, produced the following letter:
Definite allegations of participation in political activity have been made against the following three employees who are employed in the Cheticamp side of the park in seasonal positions. These are Alex P. Boudreau, George P. LeBlanc and Peter H. Poirier. These men should be released immediately and replacements obtained on the advice and recommendations of the local adviser.
There is a query over the signature because apparently they could not read it but they have taken it to be "B. M. Strong". I am not altogether surprised that they could not read the signature. The letter continues:
If getting out to vote on election day is considered being engaged in political activities, then we must of course plead guilty. However, we were not aware that federal government employees had as yet been deprived of their right to vote. As to other political activities, we are prepared to swear that neither of us, while employed by the federal government has ever given publicly any indication as to which side he was on. Our only guilt would seem to stem from the fact that we were appointed by a Liberal administration. Furthermore, we are prepared to provide you with a sworn statement bearing the signatures of 500 people in this community to the effect that nobody really knows which way we voted in the last election.
I would hope that would be true.
A dismissal of this type is a black mark against our reputation which we are not prepared to ignore. Unless your department acts immediately to erase it, we shall be forced to have recourse to legal means.
Yours very truly,
George P. LeBlanc, Alex P. Boudreau.
The minister stated in reply to my question -I want to be very exact-"the dismissal in each case was made on the basis of a declaration by an hon. member that the employee had taken an active part in politics." I am not going to repeat now what the hon. member for Laurier said earlier in the session, but he indicated the historic reasons for permitting dismissals in this fashion, a procedure,
I may say, which I, like the hon. member for Laurier, think is antiquated and should be discontinued, no matter who is in office. People should not be dismissed on the simple declaration of a member of parliament that he knows these persons to have been engaged in political activities.
The hon. member for Laurier read a lot of authorities, Sir Robert Borden, Mr. Meighen, Mr. Mackenzie King and a good many others, to the effect that the reason a declaration by a member of parliament was accepted and a declaration by anyone else was not accepted was that such a declaration could be debated right here in parliament in the face of the accuser. The minister did not tell us what member of parliament it was who made this

declaration. It does seem to me that the very least the minister could do in this case is to tell us what member made this written declaration, because it has to be a written declaration, and table it in the house so that every hon. member will have the opportunity to see it, so that we, who are responsible to all the taxpayers of Canada for the way in which public moneys are expended, will have the full and proper opportunity to see what in fact the situation is that is alleged by the hon. member and so that he, whoever he may be, will have the opportunity to defend his conduct.
I agree with what was said the other evening by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I agree completely that this procedure is something that belongs to another age. I do not care whether it was done by Liberals or Conservatives. I do not think it should be done any longer. I have no hesitation in saying that and I have no hesitation in adding that I was not aware of this practice during the time I have been a member of parliament until after June 10, 1957.

I want to repeat that I am not seeking to condemn any previous governments or any previous politicians, but I think this is the type of practice about which I should like to see the Prime Minister or anyone else undertake a reform. I should like to see investigations of these charges of political activity conducted by some impartial person. So far as I am concerned, I hope I never belong to a government in the future that carries on this practice. There may be many hon. members who think that is not a very serious thing for me to say because my political prospects are not very good.
However, I am serious about this matter, and I do not want to be diverted from the point. The point is that the minister allowed two employees to be fired from a national park, on his own statement, because some unnamed hon. member in this house made accusations. We know nothing about them, and again I say I believe we in this house are entitled to have that information so that we can form a judgment as to whether or not that was justified. These people say it was not. I am not taking their part. I have never seen these men in my life. I do not know anything whatever about them, except what I have before me here.
This is not an isolated case, of course. The minister has had other instances, and I want to say something about another one about which the minister did not bring down a return until just after his estimates were through. Before that, however, I have another letter here signed by Thomas Williams and William Asseff of Smelt Brook, Victoria county, Cape Breton. This was written on August 28, and it reads:
I know you are not the member for Victoria-Cape Breton North-but I am writing this letter to you to see if you can help us to get our jobs back on the Cape Breton Highlands national park.
I, Thomas Williams, of Smelt Brook, and William Asseff of South Harbour, Victoria county, were laid off our jobs on the 26th of August at 12 o'clock. There were two more men hired in our position that were on another job at the launchway at Smelt Brook.
Peter A. Macintosh went to work on the launchway on the 26th of August and was hired on the park on the same day. Mr. Ernest Briand who was sub-foreman on the launchway was given one or

Supply-Finance
two weeks to have someone placed as foreman so he could work with the national parks.
I ask you, sir, is this a fair way for a free Canadian to be treated or are we going to have the privilege of a free vote taken away from us.
I ask then why, when there's no complaints in the superintendent's office, were we laid off our jobs and two more men hired in our place. I ask, Mr. Member, will you ask this in parliament and send me the answers?

I want to go to another case, and this is a case which was discussed on the minister's estimates on the last evening they were before the house. He told me I would find the answers to my questions, which he did not answer-I should not say he refused to answer them, except by remaining in his seat-when this return was brought down. It was a return to a motion made by the hon. member for Ottawa West and it related to the dismissal, as I put it, or the failure to re-engage, as the minister put it at one point though he changed his ground as he went along, of a certain Mrs. A. E. Woodman of Jasper.
I have here this return and the first letter on this file is a letter to the superintendent of the national park from Mrs. Woodman, which is dated January 6. I will only read the text of the letter, and not the names, but I shall read the full text.
Having been an attendant at the Jasper information bureau for several summers, perhaps a formal application is not necessary. However, just for the record, I shall be available for service on June 1st, 1958 or earlier if required.
To this, Mrs. Woodman received the following reply dated January 21:
Thank you for your letter of January 6th making application for employment at the Jasper information bureau this summer.
We will be pleased to have you back again at the bureau this year and you will be contacted at a later date as to when your duties will commence.
That is the whole letter. Then, on June 2, and this is the next letter on the file, there is a letter addressed to Mr. Strong, chief of the national parks service, Norlite building, Ottawa. It reads:
For the past four years I have been on the summer staff at the information bureau here. This year

I applied and was accepted quite early in the year. Yesterday Mr. Pettis informed me that, in a letter from Dr. Horner, M.P. for Jasper-Edson, he received orders to discharge me because my name was associated with the Liberal party. Dr. Horner told him who was to replace me. Will you give this matter your attention, please, it is now too late for me to secure other summer work; my husband is a world war I veteran and we live on a small C.N.R. pension-he was refused work this year too but no reason given. Are we living in a Gestapo age? An early reply will be appreciated.
Then, on June 9, Mrs. Woodman wrote the minister in the following terms:
May I ask for your consideration? I Shall be as brief as possible.
Are you aware that patronage has reared its ugly head in Jasper national park?
I am not a civil servant but for the past four years I have given satisfactory service as an attendant in the information bureau here.
This year I applied for the same position early in the year and was given a letter of acceptance. On June 2, 1 was informed that Dr. Horner, M.P. for Jasper-Edson had objected to me being given employment as I was an active member of the Liberal organization in Jasper.
Mr. Pettis gave me a letter which stated-[DOT]
Perhaps I do not need to read that again because I read it. Then the letter goes on:
I understand Mr. Pettis' position-
Perhaps I should read that because I am breaking the continuity.
Mr. Pettis gave me a letter which stated, "I have been instructed by my head office in Ottawa to withdraw our offer of employment to you in the Jasper information bureau for the forthcoming season". I understand Mr. Pettis' position but this letter gives a wrong impression-I was never "offered" employment in the bureau, I applied in writing and was accepted in writing; I was informed that my work would start June 14, 1958- therefore I was discharged, most unfairly, too late in the season to secure another employment.
My husband is a veteran of world war I and we live on a small C.N.R. pension: he applied for the attendant's job at the park west gate but he was not given work of any kind-why? We can only assume that he too is being penalized for my political associations.
We have lived in Jasper for sixteen years and I feel sure, Mr. Hamilton, that you and other members of the cabinet believe in justice and a square deal for every "fellow Canadian" of Mr. Diefen-baker's.
Will you investigate this matter of my discharge from the service? I will appreciate hearing from you.
To this, the minister replied on June 14 in the following terms:
I wish to acknowledge and thank you for your letter of June 9th.
It has been government policy for many years to discharge or not employ people who have actively participated politically. By your own admission you state in your letter, "We can only assume that he too is being punished for my political associations." Under the circumstances, I have no choice in the matter but to concur with the action taken by my departmental officials.
Then there is another letter here of June 19 to Mr. Pettis from Mrs. Woodman which

I do not think I will read because it talks about getting legal advice and so on. Then there are several letters from the Liberal candidates to which reference was made by the minister. I am not going to take any more time to read this file because it is, of course, the property of the house and is available to everyone to read. After I had raised this matter in the house I received a letter from Mrs. Woodman whom I have never met and whom I do not know at all, on August 19 in the following terms:
Dear Mr. Pickersgill:
Thank you for bringing my ease out in the open and insisting on an admission from Mr. Hamilton that I was hired and then "told later not to report".
I am sending you copies of my letters from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, including my acceptance for work at the information bureau and my discharge, written in such a way that it gives the impression that an offer of work had just casually been withdrawn: nothing could be more wrong-I was never "offered" work-I asked for it and was discharged just twelve days before I expected to begin work, too late to get other full time summer employment here.
The enclosed copy of a letter from Dr. Hugh Horner, M.P. for Jasper-Edson, is a masterpiece of contradiction, it was not marked "confidential" so I do not hesitate to pass it on to you to be used as you see fit.
I have been a member of the Liberal party all my "voting" life and I just hope I am still around to do my small bit when the next election comes around.
Thank you again for your support.

Ottawa, June 9, 1958.
Mrs. A. E. Woodman,
Jasper, Alberta.
Dear Mrs. Woodman:
The Prime Minister has requested that I reply to your letter of June 2nd-
This astonished me and I put a motion on the order paper asking for the correspondence between Mrs. Woodman and the Prime Minister and the Prime Minister offered no objection to the motion which was passed. But I inquired this morning and the correspondence had not yet been tabled. I am not seeking to make anything of that fact at all. I know what preoccupations there have been. The rest of the letter follows:
Supply-Finance
The Prime Minister has requested that I reply to your letter of June 2nd, which was addressed to him with regard to the position on the tourist information bureau at Jasper.
When asked for recommendations to fill these positions I found that I could not accept your name because of your political activity. For the record I would like it to be known that the Conservative party do not intend to practice patronage as the old Liberal regime did.
I think there is a beautiful irony there.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

I continue:
We feel that a person's politics should not be of any influence in being accepted for any position. However, the general rule is that any employee of the government, civil servant or otherwise, should not take part in any political activity.
Yours sincerely,
Hugh M. Horner, M.D., M.P.
That is the whole of that letter. What I want to say is this. This lady was not employed by the government at the time of the general election. It is true that she had applied for a position and had been told that in June a casual position, a summer seasonal position, would be hers. She was a free citizen, not an employee of the government all during the election campaign. She surely had a right, if she wanted to, to engage in political activities just as any other free citizen has. The day when free citizens are not going to be allowed to engage in political activity is a day that I am sure neither the Prime Minister nor the minister on reflection wants to see happen here. If it is going to be said that no one is to be employed subsequently in the public service because he has engaged in political activity, there are a great many employees who would never be engaged in the public service. It seems to me to be an absolutely preposterous suggestion to say that because someone has been active politically and subsequently applies for a position, that should make any difference whatsoever in that position.
I quite agree with the view that a public servant, while a public servant, should not engage in political activity. I do not agree with the view that is expressed by some parties that they should. But the idea that people should be penalized because when they were not public servants they engaged in political activity seems to me to be wholly preposterous. Before we grant any more money to the minister I think we are entitled to have from him an explanation of these two cases.
I admit he has had no notice here of this other case. I would not want to press that one because I admit that the minister has not heard of it before. I do not want to be

Supply-Finance
unfair. But of these two cases the minister has had ample warning and ample knowledge, namely the cases of these two gentlemen George Leblanc and Alexander Boudreau in the Cape Breton Highlands park. I think we should have the declaration of the member of parliament who is responsible for this laid before us and read into the record so that we know what we are talking about. In the case of Mrs. Woodman I think we should hear from the minister what justification he thinks there is for penalizing people because at a time when they were not public servants they engaged in political activity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As my name has already been mentioned in this discussion, I want to say that I am indeed shocked by the practice that apparently is being followed. I do not think members of parliament should be given the right or the responsibility of informing on public employees and recommending that they be dismissed and that the government should subsequently take that recommendation as full reason for dismissing such an employee. Surely it is part of the fundamental right of every Canadian, if he is to be dismissed from a position, to know why he has been dismissed and he should have some recourse of appeal. Members of parliament should not be given this right to jettison the economic position of Canadians and to interfere in their personal right of employment if they are giving good service.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate at one point in his remarks said that he would not say that what has been done is wrong but he would say that it is antiquated. I am quite prepared to say that it is wrong. Not only is it antiquated but it is wrong. It is wrong on moral grounds. It is wrong from the standpoint of efficient government administration. It can do nothing but undermine the morale of public employees. If this practice is carried on of a member of parliament informing the minister and having people fired, it makes a mockery out of any other move by this parliament by way of a bill of rights. If parliament is sincere- and I believe it is-in wanting a bill of rights to guarantee human freedoms, then the practice of this government in this regard strikes at the very foundation of human freedoms in this country.
I can tell the government that if they continue this practice and if individual members of parliament on the government side of the house accept this as a prerogative and exercise it they will be hounded by members of the opposition in this house, session in and session out, because this is a matter of great importance to the welfare and to the
[Mr. Plckersgill.l
freedom of the people of Canada, and we are not going to take this kind of interference with human freedoms without a continuous and energetic protest.
