maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member knows I have not the file before me but it is true she was employed for the previous four or five years in the reception booth of the park and in June she certainly would be on duty. I think, therefore, the member was wrong in bringing up this matter on this vote, which has nothing to do with it and he has not achieved the purpose which he would like to have achieved. You cannot make the people of Canada swallow this idea that now the Liberals are in opposition they have suddenly changed their spots and have become as virtuous as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would lead us to believe.
This government by its actions has alleviated the problems of the civil servants and has raised the civil service level and that of the casual workers of the government to a new high, and I would say that I hope this will be the end of the subject.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the minister give us the name of the member on whose recommendation the action was taken in the Cape Breton Highlands case?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, that hon. member was the member for Inverness-Richmond.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have been listening with considerable interest and amusement to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in his remarks about political patronage. He mentioned two people who asked him to reinstate them, and I would inform him that dozens of people in Hastings South have asked me to get them reinstated in jobs they lost in 1935. They were fired in 1935 without a trial and without any consideration, and they now want to get their jobs back which were lost during a Liberal regime. I think he has made an error today because his party were past

Supp ly-A griculture
masters in this sort of thing. As far as the hon. member for Assiniboia is concerned, he has no sins to answer for as he has never had the opportunity.

Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Terminable services-
663. To provide for payments to western grain producers of $1 per acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $40,000,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I seem to detect some eagerness on the part of some hon. members to speak on this item which is to provide the money to make these payments of $1 an acre to western farmers up to $200 per farm.
The Prime Minister made a detailed statement on this matter a week ago today in which he made reference to the long term farm program on which we are engaged. He pointed to the part which this particular proposal is intended to play, and he also discussed the scheme itself in some detail. For these reasons I do not think I should take up the time of the committee for too long in speaking on the matter today.
However, I should like to say that the government gave very long and detailed consideration to the problems of western grain producers. The western members of parliament in this party-and they constitute all the hon. members concerned except one- were consulted on numerous occasions with regard to this question and they gave us very valuable advice in connection with it.
The so-called deficiency payments which were asked for by the western wheat pools and by other western farm organizations were considered very thoroughly. I say "so-called deficiency payments" and I would just like to say a word on that. These requests made by the wheat pools and other western organizations were not, strictly speaking, for deficiency payments at all. I am sorry about the confusion that exists over the term "deficiency payments". A deficiency payment is one which is made to make up the price to a certain predetermined level if the price falls below that level. This is one of the three methods used under the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act in order to put floor prices into effect. As I say, the request was not for a deficiency payment of this sort but for the fixed payment of so much a bushel on the two previous past crops.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the minister say whether or not the proposition of the wheat pools was based on a formula and, if so, how this formula was arrived at, because my understanding is that they had a definite formula.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is correct, but it has nothing to do with the point I am making now, that it was not a request for deficiency payments. What I am trying to do is to clear up the confusion that exists over the term.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It would be appreciated by the Chair if members kept their voices a little lower. There is far too much noise in the committee at the present moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As I said, the request of the western farm organizations for this payment was very carefully studied and it presented two very grave disadvantages. First of all, under payments of the kind requested, the people who would receive the largest benefits would be the largest producers, and the people who would get the smallest benefit would be those who needed help most, that is, the smaller producers. In addition, those who were hailed out or who lost their crops by any other means would receive no payment at all under the so-called deficiency payments requested, and people who had fed the major portion of their grain to livestock would similarly receive no payment. Those are very serious disadvantages. It would not make for a fair distribution, and it would not give the major portion of the money to the people who needed it most.
A second serious disadvantage is that if this payment had been put into effect with respect to oats and barley there is no question but that the United States would have reacted in one of two ways. Either that country would have placed an embargo against the entry of Canadian oats and barley into the United States or it would have been required by its own customs act to place against Canadian oats and barley a countervailing duty equivalent to the amount of the deficiency payments. Thus we would have been no better off than before. In fact, we would have been much worse off. That situation is one which made payments of the sort requested highly undesirable; it was the type of thing which would actually have done the Canadian western economy more harm than good.
The plan of acreage payments which we propose under this item is the best method, I think, which could possibly have been devised to meet the cash difficulty which it is admitted exists in western Canada is due to two short crops, a short crop this year and a short crop last year. I think it must be borne in mind that farmers, and grain farmers in particular, depend on two things: the size of the crop produced and the price received per bushel. During this year and last year the number of bushels produced have been considerably reduced and income has therefore been reduced, even though the

price was similar to that of previous years. In fact, the price is down a little, too. But 1 think we must always keep in mind that the most important determining factor is the size of the crop. It is much better, for example, to have a 40-bushel crop and get $1 a bushel than to have a 10-bushel crop and to get $2 a bushel for it.
As a result of short crops the small farmers particularly in western Canada have had very little grain to deliver. The acreage payment which we propose to put in effect will give most assistance to these small farmers who need assistance most at the present time. In commenting on the statement made by the Prime Minister, the only criticism made by the Leader of the Opposition with regard to this scheme was, really, that it was not based on any formula or principle. This is not the case. The principle upon which these payments are based is to extend the greatest amount of assistance to those who need it most, that is, to the small farmers. That is the basic principle underlying this type of payment and, of course, there is a definite formula. The formula is to make payments of $1 an acre up to a maximum of 200 acres in order to accomplish the purpose which I have enunciated in stating the principle of the proposal.
The fact that it will accomplish this purpose can I think be shown by considering the size of farms in western Canada. This is a matter which was raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and I will comment on his statement later. As reported in Hansard for October 28, 1957, at page 462 I gave a breakdown of the number of cultivated acres-the size of farms in western Canada as far as cultivated acreage is concerned-and looking at that table we see there are, or were, in that area, 230,854 permit book holders and of these, 31,299 had less than 100 cultivated acres, that is, 13 per cent of the total had less than 100 cultivated acres. The next group are those having between 100 and 199 cultivated acres, and they amount to 63,272 of these farmers, that is, 27 per cent. If you add those two groups together you have 94,571, or over 40 per cent of all the permit book holders among farmers in western Canada who have less than 200 acres in cultivation. You have a large number of others in the next group, 200 to 299 acres. The total amounts to 51,000 people in this category, but a large number of those in this group probably little more than 200 acres in cultivation. As a matter of fact, their average is 246 acres.
Taking these figures altogether I think it becomes clear that this type of payment provides payment on the total acreage in
Supply-Agriculture
cultivation of over 40 per cent of all the farmers in western Canada and provides payment on nearly all up to 50 per cent. That seems to me to be much the fairest way in which assistance could be provided to western farmers and their admitted cash deficiency made up at this time.
The hon. member for Assiniboia in commenting on the statement made by the Prime Minister stated that this payment which was going to be made was less than 10 per cent of what the farm organizations out there had requested. That is a completely incorrect statement and I am surprised at the hon. member for making that remark and another statement with which I shall deal in a moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is absolutely true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The wheat pools requested total payments amounting to $228 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On one year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, covering the two crop years, and the payment being made of course, is very much more than 10 per cent of that.
The hon. member for Assiniboia in complaining about the size of this payment also made the statement that the average cultivated acreage of farms in Saskatchewan exceeded 500 acres, a statement which I questioned at the time and which is completely incorrect. I have before me figures as to the average size of cultivated acreage for western farms. In Manitoba it is 232 acres, in Saskatchewan it is 392 acres and in Alberta it is 299 acres. Those are the average sizes of farms in the three prairie provinces. In other words, the size of the farms out there is much smaller than the average person particularly in eastern Canada always seems to believe and smaller than the hon. member for Assiniboia, who should have known better, stated.
There are one or two other points I should like to make. There were some complaints made in western Canada stirred up particularly by hon. members of the opposition parties that the Agricultural Stabilization Act affected eastern farmers far more than it affected western farmers because western wheat, oats and barley were not included under the act. That is true only to the extent that some people in western Canada specialize in the growing of grain and do not produce livestock, dairy products and so forth. I might point out that the payment being made to those western farmers now will certainly at least balance up the payments made to other farmers under this act from which a number of farmers have received no benefit because they grow nothing except wheat.
In connection with this point, however, I should emphasize that the amount of benefit

Sup p ly-A griculture
Which accrues from the Agricultural Stabilization Act cannot be measured by the actual amount of money which is being paid out under that act. As an example, take the case of butter. The amount of money we pay out in order to keep the price of butter at its present level bears no relationship whatever to the great benefit that price confers on all of the 69 per cent of Canadian farmers who are engaged in the dairy business. The same thing applies to any other payment made under the Agricultural Stabilization Act or otherwise in order to assist the agricultural industry. The benefits which derive are very much wider than the actual amount of money involved.
In closing I might just say that the money which will be paid out under this scheme will be distributed by the Canadian wheat board on the basis of the cultivated acreage shown in the current permit books for 1958. The Canadian wheat board has the organization, the set-up and facilities and the information to be able to make these payments more efficiently and expeditiously than any other agency.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister would, I am sure, be very disappointed if I did not say a few words at this time on this item of his estimates but I will do my best not to detain the committee. There are some things, however, that I feel it is necessary to say in regard to what is involved in this item, not in terms of policy, I suggest-because it does not represent policy-but in terms of short term, short range action, how it will be applied and what it covers. In so far as these payments will help to make up for declining farm income and put in circulation extra dollars where they are sorely needed then they meet our approval and will secure our support.
We have put forward, although not in this house, our own views in connection with agricultural policy. There will be an occasion, if not this session then next session, for us to discuss our views in this house because the Prime Minister last Saturday indicated that in the next session we would hear from the government in regard to long range agricultural policies. Certainly that is not involved in this item today. That is one of the reasons for which we criticized it. Furthermore, this action by the government must be a disappointment to western grain producers in the light of statements that have been made by spokesmen of the present government during recent years. Such a reaction of disappointment is natural and inevitable in view of the policies put forward by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture when they were in opposition.

The Prime Minister's policy in those days as stated in the House of Commons was to overcome by government action-in so far as it should be done by government action-the cost-price squeeze, to restore to the farmer a fair share of the national income based upon a formula of parity, taking into account the relationship between the cost of production on the one hand and the prices farmers must pay on the other.
Notwithstanding what the Minister of Agriculture has said the payments provided in this item are based on no discernible or rational principle. If there is any principle involved it is only a one based on a grant to be made to people who need it and for short term. There is no principle involved in this item which is of a general application over a period of years. Certainly this grant is not related to cost of production or prices and it is not related to any principle of parity. Indeed, when the Prime Minister referred to this matter a week ago today he did not even mention the idea, the principle of parity although he did in that statement dismiss the principle of deficiency payments and the principle-if it is a principle-of a two-price system.
The references to parity made by the Prime Minister on previous occasions were certainly absent last Saturday and they were absent from the statement made today by the Minister of Agriculture. Instead, we were subjected to some general statements and philosophical observations in the statement made by the Prime Minister concerning the difficulties of agriculture and the necessity of the government doing something about it next session on a long term basis. When I speak about the precise language the Prime Minister used with respect to this matter in the past, I have in mind in particular the words he used in the house on March 12, 1956. As found on page 2021 of Hansard, the present Prime Minister had this to say:
The squeeze which the farmer suffers results from the disparity in the relationship between the prices of farm products and the prices the farmer has to pay. When they are in proper relationship parity is established, and it is parity that the farm organizations across this country are asking for today. Not charity but parity.
Those were the words of the present Prime Minister at that time. I suggest that in the action taken by the government on this occasion the farmers are getting neither charity nor parity. Certainly the Prime Minister made no effort last Saturday to relate his payments to a formula for parity about which he spoke in such feeling terms in the debate to which I have referred. In the speech from which I have just quoted the Prime Minister defined parity and left no doubt in the minds

of those of us who were in the house at that time that the establishment of a system of parity prices would prove a solution to the problem of agriculture. Indeed, as found at page 2026 of Hansard for the same day, the Prime Minister moved an amendment in these words:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
That same theme was developed in the election campaign of 1957. I find it necessary at this time to refer only to a few of the Prime Minister's speeches in that campaign. Some of them have already been referred to in the house. According to the Ottawa Journal of May 9, 1957, the Prime Minister told a Brantford audience that the Conservatives if elected will "maintain a flexible price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers, based on a fair price-cost relationship". I take it that the prairie farmers were not excluded from that reference. Then, on April 25, 1957, in his opening speech in that campaign the Prime Minister outlined an agricultural policy. I quote from the press statement that was issued:
We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income-
"We will assure".
-by maintaining a flexible-and I underline the word "flexible"-
These are the Prime Minister's words.
-price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on a fair price-cost relationship.
It is fair to conclude from that, of course, that the Prime Minister had the western producer in mind as well as other agricultural producers. Last session the Minister of Agriculture introduced his agricultural stabilization measure and defended it as fulfilling all the election pledges of his party.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And it did.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In the light of what I have just quoted, in the light of the Prime Minister's statement in the house in 1956 when he advocated an agricultural policy based on parity prices, and he defined what parity prices were and I have given the definition, how can the Minister of Agriculture say that the agricultural stabilization measure introduced last session fulfilled all the election pledges of his party? The minister in explaining that legislation, and I refer to Hansard for December 14, 1957, page 2398,
Supply-Agriculture
stated that a guaranteed price could be provided through purchase of the commodity, paying deficiency payments, and other price support payments determined by the governor in council. What has happened to these deficiency payments? On Saturday last the Prime Minister dismissed deficiency payments for western agriculture because they, and I quote from page 4346 of Hansard of this session, "are not in the long run interest of either the western grain producer or the nation as a whole."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I just finished explaining that they are not deficiency payments; these are flat payments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: They are indeed. I am just trying to explain that the agricultural policy of the government when it was in opposition and when it was talking about policy during the election campaign was a policy based on parity and deficiency payments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have deficiency payments in effect for a large number of commodities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not think even the ingenuity of the Minister of Agriculture will be able to prove to the house that the action embodied in this item and the policy they have adopted up to the present in regard to agriculture meets the promises made by the Prime Minister and himself during the election campaign and previously in the house. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, last Saturday when the Prime Minister spoke there was no clarion call for parity. There was no ringing declaration for deficiency payments. There was no formula to guarantee a cost-price relationship, no principle advanced to produce a fair share of the national income for the farmer. And that is what my hon. friends talked about so much during the election campaign and previously in the house.
Therefore we are now entitled to ask the Prime Minister whether he has repudiated his election promises to the prairie farmers on this matter. We are entitled as well to point out that the agricultural policy for the western farmer proposed by the Prime Minister when in opposition is now a virtual shambles. I have no doubt the hon. member for Assiniboia will be able to help me confirm that fact when he gets up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You should speak about a shambles and promises.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Deficiency payments are out. Parity is out. A fair share of the national income is not mentioned. What is to be the substitute? This one-shot operation which when it ends, so far as we know, is to be replaced by what? We do not know. We do know that it is not based on any kind of

Supply-Agriculture
principle enunciated in the house or throughout the country by the Prime Minister or Minister of Agriculture. We remind the Prime Minister of his statement in the house that he was laying down as an agricultural policy for the Conservative party of that day "not charity but parity".
I will conclude, Mr. Chairman, by referring to one editorial expression of opinion on this matter, not from the Winnipeg Free Press although they have some interesting references to it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is where your speech came from; your speech has the appearance of Winnipeg Free Press authorship.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: My right hon. friend is really almost morbidly and unhealthily preoccupied by what the Winnipeg Free Press says. Why does he worry so much about the Winnipeg Free Press?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Because apparently it is my hon. friend's adviser in all things.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am glad the Prime Minister said "apparently" because that, of course, covers almost any statement he can make. I am sure he really thinks that it is more apparent than real. However, I would not hesitate to take good economic advice from whatever source I could get it, and I commend that to my right hon. friend and to the Minister of Finance. I certainly do not know where he is getting his agricultural advice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You had better go to another source if you want good economic advice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not know where he is getting his advice at the present time but it is not really very impressive when what results from it is this one-shot $40 million operation which as far as it goes will help the grain producers but will leave them high and dry as to what is going to happen in the future. The Toronto Globe and Mail is not a paper normally too friendly to our party but in commenting on this particular vote in its issue of September 4 it had this to say:
Its effect will be neither prophylactic nor therapeutic-it will prevent nothing, neither will it cure. It will do little, considering the price of farmland and tractors, to help him increase the size of his establishment. And rather than protect him from inflation, it will subject him and everybody else to more inflation, because he will not produce with it, just consume.
Then, this editorial ends with these words:
Isn't it time, in short that they stopped looking upon the small farmer, and the small farmer stopped looking upon himself, as a charity case?
I am sure the small farmer does not look upon himself as a charity case, but I am not so sure the government does not look

upon the small farmer in this sense if this is the best he can get from the government on agricultural policy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amount of money that is involved in this item, and the absence of any formula based on the cost of production, means that the government has abandoned the many promises it made to the Canadian people over the years to provide a system of prices based on parity. The members of the government, for many years, have said to the farmers of this country that if they were elected they would immediately embark upon a policy that would provide such parity prices. This policy-this lack of policy -demonstrates that the Conservative party has finally abandoned the principle of parity and, in the words of the Minister of Agriculture himself, is not providing even deficiency payments to the prairie grain producers.
The type of payment that is being provided by this motion is the worst possible type of payment that could be made. It is a bad type of payment because it is inapplicable, because it is not based on a formula tied to the cost of production, and because it smacks of a handout. The government's position in the past has been very clear. The Conservative party had a handbook in the 1957 election, entitled "Agriculture"-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And very good.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is very good; before the election what they said was wonderful, but since the election the performance-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Wonderful, too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-ten per cent. The handbook
says:
Regular motions have been introduced into the house by Mr. Diefenbaker in order to secure for the farmer a more satisfactory share of the national income. April 8, 1941:
"Immediate steps should be taken to create a parity of prices as between agriculture and other products in order to improve the position of Canadian agriculture so that it may receive a just and fair return."
On March 23, 1953, another motion by the Prime Minister:
Consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers of a fair price-cost relationship.
Where is the floor price for wheat, oats and barley based on the fair price-cost relationship? It is nonexistent. As a matter of fact, the floor price gets worse every year in terms of purchasing power. In recent years the initial prices with the exception of oats, which was reduced a couple of years ago, have remained the same and every year the cost of production goes up. On March 12, 1956, just two years ago the Prime

Minister moved in this house a motion that legislation should be introduced to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers of a fair price-cost relationship. I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture believes in parity prices? Does the minister believe that there should be a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure a fair price-cost relationship? I do not think he does.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We provided that in the stabilization bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
A parity of prices-what an emasculation of the English language. Parity prices, which are based on equity, which are based on a price formula related to the cost of production, but what the minister has brought in is a bill, a so-called stabilization bill, that provides floors on a moving average based on market prices. He calls that parity prices. The Prime Minister, speaking at Kipling, May 17, 1957, is reported in the Regina Leader-Post as having said that by electing the Conservative party the farmers would get parity prices, cash advances on farm-stored grain. Cash advances have been provided and the farmers want to know when the promise to provide parity prices will be implemented.
The Minister of Agriculture has quarrelled with the term "deficiency payments", as being used by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. He says that what they are asking for is a flat payment. I do not care whether he wishes to call it a flat deficiency payment or some other kind of a deficiency payment, but it is much more adequate than anything the government is proposing in this legislation. It is based on a precise formula, that is that there shall be a deficiency payment sufficient to bring prices up to the level that prevailed over the eight-year period from 1947 to 1955. The Saskatchewan wheat pool pointed out that since 1947 the cost of production has gone up by 50 per cent, while the price of wheat has fallen by 21 per cent. They are not asking for parity prices. If they were asking for parity prices, they would probably be asking for well over $2 a bushel. They are not asking for any compensation because of the increase in the cost of production, even though the increased cost of production has been more than 50 per cent. However, they are asking that there shall be protection of their returns so that with the tremendous increase in the cost of production year after year, they do not have to take a lower and lower price in the succeeding years.
They are not asking for a continuing price but a floor price based on an eight-year average from 1947 to 1955. If the farmers were given everything for which they asked they would still be hard-pressed in meeting
Supply-Agriculture
this rapid increase in the cost of production. The Saskatchewan wheat pool is heading this drive requesting a deficiency payment of 27 cents a bushel for the 1955-56 wheat crop and a deficiency payment of 36 cents a bushel for the 1956-57 wheat crop. The minister says that the legislation he is providing will do more for the people who need it most. I challenge that statement. I do not think it is correct. The Saskatchewan wheat pool, in their proposition, would provide a basis of payment relating to the marketing of grain up to a maximum of $1,500 per farmer, depending upon the amount of grain that he has produced.
The Minister of Agriculture went on to say that the reason the government is doing this is not because of any change in the cost of production; it is not because of any fall in price levels, but it is because of a short crop last year and this year. Then, the minister says farm income depends on the size of the crop. This is not as correct as saying that farm income depends on marketings. If the farmer markets more grain, he gets more money. Farm marketings have not been low in recent years, and have not been low in this period to which the farm organizations allude. As a matter of fact, even in the year that has just passed there was more wheat marketed than in the long term average. The wheat pool has this to say:
Moreover, in the last five years while the agricultural problem has been building up, western farmers have delivered more wheat to country elevators than they have on the average for the last 35 years. Canadian exports, likewise, have been above the long-term average in the last two years...
In short, western farmers have been selling better than average crops during these years of surplus. And they have found, nevertheless, that the cost-price squeeze is forcing them into bankruptcy.
That is a very strong term. Does the minister think that $200 will save the farmers from bankruptcy?
The disparity between farm costs and farm prices is the major problem. Farm groups are suggesting that it be solved by deficiency payments on wheat, oats and barley delivered during the crop years 1955-56 and 1956-57.
The Prime Minister has offered them a dollar an acre up to $200. In making his statement announcing the $40 million he outlined what he called a comprehensive long term agricultural program. I do not think there was anything really new in it. I do not think there is anything in it that meets the basic problem of the farmer's rising cost of production and falling prices for grain. The first problem the Prime Minister talked about was wheat exports as well as promotion and market development. Yet in recent years we have been marketing more than an

Supply-Agriculture
average crop each year and exporting more than an average crop while the farmers go bankrupt. So continuing our exports at the good levels of previous years is not going to correct this problem of the price-cost squeeze.
Then the second plank is a comprehensive crop insurance program. I would be most pleased if such a program were brought about. But what does crop insurance mean? It means at the very best that the farmers will get a smaller income in time of crop failure than if they had a crop. Hence at the very best it will give them less money than when they have a crop. They have had good crops. They have sold good crops. Yet they are going broke. A crop insurance program is not going to cure that situation.
The third point, a food bank for deficit areas in time of crop failure. That is a good program. That is part of sound agriculture. But it does not meet the current price cost squeeze at all.
The fourth plank is long term program of farm loans. That above all will not solve the farm problem. The farmers in western Canada now are much more concerned about paying the debts they have than about getting more debts. While long term credit at low interest rates will be of value in building an economic unit, it is certainly no cure for the problem at hand.
The fifth plank is the means of meeting the small farm problem which the government has talked so much about. The government has under consideration ways and means of improving the level of living of farmers on small farms by means of better land use. That will not do very much. The farmer on a small farm is probably the best authority about how to use his land most efficiently and he is using it efficiently. He is using it so efficiently that he has marketed the biggest crop in history in recent years. So that is not going to get him out of this mess.
The government is going to encourage the formation of economic farm units. The problem is that we have the small farm. Now they say they are going to get him a bigger farm. It means only one thing, namely that there will be fewer farmers. When you get one farmer on a bigger piece of land, there is less land for somebody else because the supply of land is fixed. When you divide it up into bigger units, you have fewer farms. So what they say is that they are going to help the small farmer by getting rid of him and leaving the land to larger farmers on economic units.
As the sixth plank, plans are already under way for a national conservation conference. Judging by the accomplishments of some

recent conferences, I do not think too much hope can be given to the producers on the basis of a conservation conference to deal with the whole question of the price-cost squeeze and the economic position of the farmer.
What has been the reaction to this in western Canada? The other day I put on the record some of the comments of Mr. James Paterson, head of the Interprovincial Farm Union Council. I notice that other prominent persons in Saskatchewan have been making statements. I have here in my hand a clipping from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of September 2. It is entitled "Ottawa 'Deficiency' Payment Piddling, Van Vliet Thinks".
-said Professor H. Van Vliet, head of the farm management department of the university, "reminds me of the Bennett nickel-payment of the 'thirties'." That is. he considered it too "piddling" to be worthy of much attention.
One of the very best agricultural economists in the province of Saskatchewan, the head of the agricultural economics department at the University of Saskatchewan, a man of many years experience in agriculture and in farm economics, a man who is not given to making exaggerated statements, calls the payment piddling. R. B. Bennett, when the pressure was on in 1931 and western grain producers were in a squeeze, brought in a payment of five cents a bushel on wheat. If the government had brought in a five cent a bushel payment on wheat for the two years that the wheat pool is asking about it would have amounted to about $35 million. That would have been almost as much as the government is now providing for; and if they had made comparable payments on oats and barley, it would be more. A five cent payment based on purchasing power of 1931, related to the quantities of wheat marketed in the years 1956-57, and extended to oats and barley, would have meant more today than the $40 million based on the $1 an acre that we have under consideration. This is no better treatment in 1958, in terms of the cost of production and the value of money and the agricultural prices, than R. B. Bennett's five cents a bushel which did the Conservative party in those years more damage than good.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Why did it do more
damage?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Because it was not enough. It was something like the $6 increase in the old age pension. Every old age pensioner was glad to get it but it was far short of what was justified and needed and it made him so angry that he voted against the people who had provided the inadequate increase.

I do not think that this payment meets the situation. I do not think it is nearly enough. The second vice president of the Saskatchewan farmers union is reported in the newspapers as saying that he is giving Saskatchewan farmers advice to take the $200 they are paid and invest it in a return railway ticket to Ottawa so that they can all come down here in a mass delegation and impress upon the government the need to provide deficiency payments in keeping with the requests of the farm organizations. This payment of a dollar an acre will mean $200, of course, to the majority of farmers. Will that solve the economic crisis which he faces? How much money is it? It is 55 cents a day.
I ask the government to consider how far 55 cents a day will go towards providing the farmer and his family with an income and how far it will go towards paying the cost of production of agriculture in this country?
The position the Prime Minister has taken in this house until recent months in advocating a system of parity prices, a system of support prices, based on a fair price-cost relationship was clearly a good one. It is just as valid today as it was in 1941 and in the subsequent years when he moved these motions. It is needed just as much now and we are apparently just as far away from getting it as we ever have been.
I would hope the government will meet the request of farm organizations for deficiency payments based on what I consider to be a reasonable formula, a system which does not ask for an ever increasing amount related to an increase in cost of production but which merely says there will be support prices which will not allow a further deterioration in the prices of wheat, oats and barley.
A few years ago we had a strenuous debate in this house at the end of the United Kingdom wheat agreement, resulting in the provision of $65 million from the national treasury into that pool. This $65 million was not then felt to be adequate from the standpoint of western farmers, but the need today is much greater than it was then because, since that time, the price of farm products has deteriorated by a very large amount.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Livestock prices are away better than they were at that time and so are dairy prices.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister did not say when his party was advocating parity prices that the parity prices for grain producers would be forgotten about if the market for cattle appeared to be improved. No, Mr. Chairman, the farmers of western Canada will not be satisfied until the government provides them with a floor price, a continuing one, at a
Sup p ly-A griculture
reasonable level and until they feel the government has fulfilled its many promises to provide parity prices. The sum of $200, as I said a few days ago, is worth just $200, and to that extent is welcome, but $1 per acre is a very small part of the amount of money necessary at this time even in the face of very large markets to give to the people on the prairies a standard of living which compares reasonably well with that of other Canadians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not want to take up the time of the committee at great length, but having listened to the two speeches made by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia, there are a number of matters to which I think reference should be made.
I have listened to my hon. friend from Assiniboia on many occasions and he is the most generous man with other people's money I have ever known. He is all for the reduction of taxes, the almost removal of income tax on average incomes, but when it comes to generous promises and statements with regard to what he would do in the circumstances, he has no equal in this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think that tribute is due to him because he brought up an example a little while ago as a passing jibe at the Liberal party, that having increased the old age pension by $6 per month they had thereby annoyed the old age pensioners who, while pleased to receive that amount, found it convenient and proper to vote against the Liberal party. I would say to the hon. gentleman that if the amount of promises resulted in votes in keeping with the exaggeration of the promises made by C.C.F. members before the last election, the numbers in his party would not have been reduced from some 25 to 8, because as I remember it those irresponsible promises indicated $75 per month for the old age pension. The people cannot be deceived by such promises which are made simply for political purposes.
One of the major reasons-and I say this with great respect to the hon. gentleman to whose advocacy I have always paid the strictest regard-for the diminution of national support for the party he represents is the irresponsible nature of the promises made by those associated with him.
I take second place to no one-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In making promises.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-in my desire to see that agriculture shall receive its fair share of the national income, and that has been the purpose and the aim of the government which I have the honour to lead. We have gone forward

Supply-Agriculture
in the last 15 or 16 months during which time we have been in office to a degree that has met with the support of farmers generally across Canada as well as other citizens.
I know it is a great tribute to us that it is expected that all the promises we made would be completely implemented within the short time we have been in power. I ask my hon. friend to go across this country and to see whether the reaction he finds is not that never before in Canada has there been in such a short period of time during which a government has been in power when so many of its promises made to the electorate of the country have been carried out.
No matter what is done, my hon. friend will always say it is not enough. This will be the case no matter what course is followed. For years he was advocating, and in this he joined with the rest of us, the Saskatchewan dam project, but when we proceeded as one of our first acts to implement our promises in that regard we receive from him that qualified approval that we have not done enough in rendering at least $75 million available to the people of Saskatchewan.
One of the first acts of this government when it assumed office was to commence a review of the agricultural policies and these studies have been productive of legislative and administrative action which has materially benefited agricultural producers in all parts of Canada. 1 point out to my hon. friend that while I am not among those who accept in their entirety the Gallup polls which are taken from time to time, since this parliament began we have received an increase in support from the farmers as well as from other citizens of Canada because this government has gone ahead in an endeavour to bring about a new concept of implementation of promises made at any time heretofore. One of the first acts of this government when it assumed office in the development of our agricultural policy was the legislation passed under the title of the Agricultural Stabilization Act which provides Canadian farmers with a degree of security they had not known before.
I should like to review briefly what this measure has achieved for Canadian farmers. As hon. members know, the Agricultural Stabilization Act provides for the mandatory stabilization of the price of nine key commodities at not less than 80 per cent of their average price for the preceding ten years. These nine commodities represent 65 per cent of the farm cash income apart from western cereal grains. This act also provides for the stabilization of prices of non-mandatory commodities at levels fixed by the governor in council.

The effective prices fixed for the mandatory commodities have been about 100 per cent of the previous ten years average for butter and cheese, 85 per cent for eggs, 84 per cent for hogs and 80 per cent for cattle, sheep and wheat, oats and barley outside the wheat board area. Then other commodities for which stabilization is not mandatory have also been brought under the act at prices reaching up to 90 per cent of the ten year average for soy beans, 93 per cent for sugar beets and 110 per cent for wool.
The steps taken under this act have been successful in preventing serious price declines in several commodities. In others they have provided a measure of price assurance for farms which has enabled them to plan their operations with a high degree of confidence.
"Done nothing", he said. "Taken no steps in a year to implement the promises." But the hon. member will remember that under the stabilization act regard is had to the cost of production so as to bring about as far as possible that degree of security for the farmer which will bear a fair relationship to the cost of production.
In so far as the prairie farmers are concerned, while support was given to the measure when it was first introduced by the hon. gentleman and by those associated with him, it was always subject to some suggestion that it was not enough or that there was something wrong with it. The hon. gentleman has fine ability but he is developing a carping attitude. No matter what is done he always has to carp, he always has to indulge in some small criticism. This is not in keeping with what he used to be, and I point this out to him as one who has listened to him throughout the years with interest and admiration. The hon. member has developed a tendency which is dangerous to one so young as he, an attitude of continual carping, a continual dealing with small things, never prepared to say that anything is right or that steps are being taken in the direction of improvement.
To meet the specific regional problems of our prairie farmers, interest-free cash advances to the amount of $34.5 million were provided to some 50,000 farmers on their farm-stored grain. I have already referred to the South Saskatchewan dam irrigation project, which is a major matter of benefit to agriculture. I can also refer to the steps that have been taken to prevent the dumping into Canada of agricultural products so as to preserve for the Canadian farmers their proper markets and to safeguard them against this type of competition which bears no relationship to actual cost. These are some of the things that we have

done. These are the courses that we have mapped out. Our objective is unchanged, namely to raise agriculture and the other economies of our country to a level in keeping with the general situation prevailing within our country and internationally.
Today the hon. member grudgingly admitted -I think it was a grudging admission, by his attitude and his manner of speech-that last year as a result of a vigorous export policy by the Department of Trade and Commerce Canadian exports of wheat rose to 317 million bushels, the highest in five years, at a time when other exporting nations had experienced major declines in their sales.
These are some of the things that we have been able to achieve in a matter of 15 months or slightly more, during a portion of which time we were absent from our duties because of an election campaign. These are some of the things which we have done. I set out the plan for the future and the course to be followed at the election as we proceeded step by step, and in the meantime made provision to assist, in particular, the small farmers by payments as provided in the estimates now before us.
I listened with interest, also, to the Leader of the Opposition. He dealt with agricultural matters. He spoke of the cost-price squeeze. I do not seem to remember that at any time when he was in a position to do something on behalf of western farmers or on behalf of farmers in general across Canada he showed anything like the enthusiasm which he is displaying today. We talk about promises. I have some here. These are the agricultural promises made by the hon. gentleman in his speeches across the country, things which could have been done, action which could have been taken during the years in which the government to which he belonged was in power. During all those years we asked for some action. Today when action is being taken and when a course is being followed which will bring about the rehabilitation of agriculture to a state which it has not enjoyed in recent years, the answer given by the hon. gentleman is that from the paper from which he quotes so frequently, or from the group of advisers who served him so ill only a few months ago by the advice they gave him then. It is an interesting attitude, the one shown by the hon. gentleman. He is ambidexterous, if I may use that expression. He says: "Oh, it is $40 million, but it is not worth while considering; it has no principle."
The principle was set forth by the Minister of Agriculture, and I set it forth the other day. It is a provision that is meant to meet an immediate situation. The amount in question is, as I stated the other day, more than the
Supply-Agriculture
amount which for so many years represented the request on the part of hon. members of the C.C.F., the amount that would have to be paid into wheat board funds in order to secure for the farmer under a two-price system a fair and proper return for that portion of his wheat production which is used in Canada.
We have taken this step. We intend to carry out by gradual stages a policy to bring about the achievement of that which we advocated through the years. My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia talks about marches on Ottawa. That is something he has been trying to get the farmers to do for months. I have read the speeches he made out there. He called on the western farmers to march on Ottawa and they told him to march back to Ottawa by himself. All over western Canada he has been bringing about that new form of democracy that consists in having the farmers march. He spoke about it again today. He said the $200 could be used by the average farmer to buy a return ticket.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It was the second vice-president of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union who made that statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has been able to produce one or two but he has not been too successful on the whole. He went out to western Canada. He talked to the farmers and urged them to march. "On to Ottawa!" was his cry, but he came back by himself.
Mr. Chairman, this is part of an agricultural policy designed, as the Minister of Agriculture said a moment ago, to meet an immediate situation. When the next session arrives we intend to introduce a measure for which the farmers have asked from the earliest days in western Canada, something which has also been requested by farmers in other parts of Canada, an insurance plan to bring about the assurance of at least a modicum of income, that degree of income which will not cost the farmer too much to assure himself of, and through which during the dark days of drought the farmer may be assured of at least a fair and reasonable rate of return. That is one of the things that came about under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That met the situation in the western provinces to a degree. That legislation was placed on the statute books as a result of the initiative of the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. It has been expanded, it has served a successful purpose and has been beneficial. Farmers generally are today asking for something further in that direction and it is because they are asking

Supp ly-A griculture
for that we intend to provide the opportunity at the next session of parliament of taking this further step.
I am not going into the question of deficiency payments. I dealt with that on the other occasion and I am not going to take the time of the committee to deal with it again. I pointed out that during the election campaign and prior thereto I had stated at no time that deficiency payments would be introduced. At no time did I directly or indirectly promise deficiency payments. What I said was that this was one of the suggestions made by the farmers that would receive the fullest and most sincere consideration. We gave it that consideration for weeks on end. We listened to the views of economists. We discussed the general situation in so far as international trade is concerned. I placed our reasons before the house when 1 mentioned the particular item of $40 million. At that time I explained that deficiency payments applied to deliveries of grain would fail to help those producers most in need and would require very large subsidies from the federal treasury.
My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia talks about 10 per cent. What he is asking for apparently is $400 million. If $40 million is being given at this time by way of advance, is it 10 per cent?-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Less than 10 per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, less than 10 per cent. Let us be reasonable. Does my hon. friend suggest that there should be made available at this time over $400 million? That is the kind of argument that brought about the situation in which he and his party find themselves today. No farmer with whom I am familiar in the western provinces has been other than reasonable throughout the years. They have not asked for the impossible. They have requested a reasonable return. I speak for the large body of those in the western provinces who throughout the years have known that when I spoke to them I have represented the facts as they were.
The government made a careful study of this matter. The serious implications for our export trade have not been answered. The subject was conveniently neglected by hon. gentlemen who have spoken. Deficiency payments to producers will be classed as a producer subsidy and grain entering export trade may be liable to countervailing duties in certain countries.
When we tried to do something on behalf of the farmer by bringing in anti-dumping legislation my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition said, "Of course I am for it, but we are against it". On both sides of the question in so far as GATT is concerned of

which he spoke so eloquently, were we to enter into the scheme that is advocated in the form in which it is suggested we would find ourselves immediately in difficulties in our export trade.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are out of order speaking about GATT.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In so far as our exports to the United States of oats and barley are concerned, as I said previously, close to 100 per cent of our export trade in oats is to the United States and one-quarter of our export trade in barley is to the United States. To bring into effect these payments on these two particular grains would result in action being taken against us which would be nothing but detrimental to the Canadian farmers as a whole.
We gave the fullest and most complete consideration to this question. I myself know something of the western farmer and his problems. I know it from those days long ago, the earliest days. I know the difficulties experienced by the farmers in those early days when we went on to land that was entirely virgin. I experienced those days and I know those difficulties. That is one of the reasons why the policies we have enunciated were designed in order to meet that condition.
We took steps at the last session in so far as cash advances are concerned and also under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. This session we took steps, as we have since we came into power, to meet the terrific competition that farmers are receiving through imports of agricultural products from other countries being dumped into the markets here to the detriment of Canadians. We have taken the necessary steps at this session. We took action with respect to rehabilitation through the South Saskatchewan river dam. In addition to that we made provision for an immediate situation. At the next session our further unfolding of the program that was enunciated will be carried out to the end that agriculture will be able to attain that position wherein a degree of fairness and justice will be assured not only to farmers in western Canada but to farmers generally throughout the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on these estimates I should like to say at the outset I am in full agreement with the principle of the motion to make payments to the western grain producers for which approval is sought in the estimates that are before us. I am grateful to the Prime Minister for introducing this legislation and to the ministers who were so instrumental in drafting a formula under which payments will

be made on an acreage basis so that every farmer will benefit. The $40 million proposed in the estimates will be of assistance to the western grain growers who have been labouring hard under the price squeeze in which they have found themselves over the last few years. One must be a grain grower to know what it means to produce under such a cost of production. Taking into consideration the so-called price squeeze that has been with us for a long time, without any attempt having been made in the past to prevent it or cope with it, this payment cannot be expected to rectify all the evils of the past. However, it is reasonable to assume that the $40 million proposed as payment for one year will have an effect on western agriculture and will alleviate some of the hardships experienced in the past. Indeed, it will go much further than the agricultural policy that we heard so much about last winter, namely the ten cent increase in the initial price which money in the first place belongs to the farmer.
Had steps been undertaken in the past or even as late as 1955 when it was apparent then as it is now that the price the farmer was receiving for his produce was away out of line proportionately with the prices he had to pay, the situation would not have been as grim as it is now. Consequently the effect of this payment at the present time would have been much more beneficial as the need would not have been as great as it is now.
With the way the situation is now it will be expected that the forthcoming payment should correct all the shortcomings of past years but it must be admitted this is almost impossible without putting too big a burden on the treasury in one year. The part I like most about the action taken, and I know it is appreciated by many farmers, is the fact that this is only one part of a long range program for Canadian agriculture. As stated by the Prime Minister, under this policy, among other benefits, the farmer will find protection from such hazards as drought, frost and crop failures of various kinds.
This is a policy which has been advocated over the years by farm organizations and authorities on agriculture. If it is implemented it is hoped it will put agriculture on a sounder economic basis. In my opinion this program will go a long way towards achieving the ultimate goal, namely to give the farmer a fair return for his investment and labour and to place him in the same position as other segments of our nation by giving him a fair return for his investment and labour.
I would be failing in my duty if in connection with this estimate I did not mention the agricultural amendments implemented during this session, namely 57071-3-300
Supply-Agriculture
P.F.A.A. cash advances and others. All these acts were amended to meet changing conditions in agriculture and I know that if changes should be necessary in the future in connection with what we are now discussing they will be forthcoming.
Finally, I should like to say that I am pleased that this estimate has been brought in at this time. If it had been introduced last winter or before March 31 it would have been classified as just election bait but now it will serve as a clear indication that the government is concerned with the welfare of all sections of our country. On behalf of the western grain growers and myself I should like to ask the house to approve the estimate before us to provide for payments to western grain producers in accordance with the regulations of the governor in council.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in replying to the Prime Minister's announcement of this policy a few days ago our leader had this to say, as found on page 4348 of Hansard for August 30:
I am thinking particularly at this moment of the fisherman who has also had his hard times, and who perhaps will look with a certain amount of envy to this kind of action taken by the government for the grain producers.
Naturally, Mr. Chairman, we do not object to this legislation but, as has been pointed out, our fishermen can suffer from the failure of the fisheries just as farmers suffer from the failure of crops. My purpose in rising at this time is to call to the minister's attention the fact that the fishery has failed this year in many parts of Newfoundland, and we hope that the same consideration and assistance will be given to the fishermen as is being given to the farmers under this legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a western farmer I had intended to take part in the discussion of this supplementary payment of $40 million to the prairie grain producers. No statement is necessary from me now. I want to thank the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture for answering opposition statements so fully. The statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture will be very carefully studied by prairie farmers and I suggest that they will be well received when considered in relation to the government's long range agricultural policy.
There is one important aspect of the government's farm policy that I should like to emphasize for a moment because it is a part of the long range program. I refer to the farm cost survey on the prairies late this fall. I want to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce on his announcement of July 19 of this farm cost survey. On July 19, as

Supply-Agriculture
found at page 2469 of Hansard, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
X believe it will meet a very great need because we are always encountering the problem of cost and income in so far as agriculture is concerned.
Such an inquiry into farm costs is greatly needed in the formulation of the government's long term agricultural policy. Such a step should have been taken years ago by the previous government. The fact that they did not undertake such a survey and did not have any definite figures explains why their agricultural policies during 22 years lacked any long range objective.
There has been a great deal of loose talk about farm costs. I say "loose talk" because definite figures are not available. When I was in Ottawa with the prices board in the 1940's the question of average farm costs was always coming up and no one had a definite answer, not even the farm organizations. I recall one conference of prices board officials with farm groups when the question of the cost of producing a bushel of wheat was raised. There were almost as many different answers as there were farmer representatives in the room.
I mention this, Mr. Chairman, in this committee to emphasize the importance of the farm cost survey this fall. The undertaking of this farm cost survey indicates the determination of this government to tackle and solve Canada's farm problems. I am sure that the prairie farmers will accept this $40 million supplementary payment in the spirit in which the government is paying it, as immediate help in a problem that can only be solved by a long range program, such as a program of better farm credit, national crop insurance, better land use and greater wheat sales, which this government is undertaking. The farm cost survey this fall is, as I said before, an indication of this government's determination to tackle the farm problem and to solve it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, I am reminded of a day many years ago in the history of our country when the minister of agriculture saw his sincere efforts to help misunderstood by those whom he sought so diligently to assist. I refer, of course, to the five-cent payment to which reference has been made in this debate, a payment that was made during the period when the Hon. Robert Weir was minister of agriculture. This payment went to the farmers who produced the grain, but did not go to farmers who did not have those bountiful crops of grain. It is for this reason we have this estimate based on an acreage payment which will go out to farm people, and which will give them something
[Mr. Pascoe.l
to make up the difference between the sale price and the cost of production.
During the past several days I have had reason to think back over the past 20 years during which I have been actively engaged in the agricultural industry. Before that, I recall doing the chores on my father's farm. I recall various responsibilities from time to time, and particularly those which resulted from service in positions which resulted in one being continually confronted with the problems of agriculture. On this occasion I should like to put on record, for this parliament and for succeeding parliaments as well, the acceptance of the government's action, with the usual reservation that they pursue this whole matter of farm security and the attempt to ensure that the people engaged in this industry shall enjoy a fair share of the national income. The Prime Minister did a creditable job today and a few days ago in presenting the overall agricultural situation in this country, that is as creditable a job as anyone could do before the report of the price spreads commission is made public and before the survey that is now being conducted into farm living costs and costs of production in these various areas of Canada where agriculture forms the basic industry is completed.
It seemed to me that as he spoke the other day, and again today, he spoke as no other man in the recent history of our industry or of our parliament has spoken on behalf of those engaged in the agricultural industry. He spoke with a feeling that came from recognition of how closely the farm people of this country are confined to overalls. This is one of the reasons why I am convinced that the legislation which will follow will be the type that will endure for many years to serve this industry that is basic to Canada's economic welfare. From the very beginning, I have been one of those who has held the view that our first consideration should be the adoption of those measures which will help to build a sound national policy and which will apply with equality to farm people in every segment of our industry and in all parts of the country.
What is of even more importance is the fact that this session has resulted in the development of some of the bases of that agricultural policy, and of equal importance is the fact that even now the remaining part of that program is only awaiting the application of a reliable basis upon which to put these things into operation for the benefit of the people in all parts of Canada. The present item ir. the estimates is a short terms measure which will be welcomed by the farmers in western Canada, especially in the light of the long

term objectives which have remained untouched over a period of years by those who today form the opposition group in parliament. I do not think that anyone in western Canada will seriously consider this assistance as peanuts, as was suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia the other day, nor do I believe his reference to it as a pittance will go down very well with many thinking farm people. At the same time, I acknowledge that does not mean that the needs of the western farmer have been fully met.
The stabilization bill fulfils a widespread need in many parts of this country, and it will become increasingly important as the production of livestock continues to increase in our province. Earlier in the estimates we had an item of $17,500,000 to reimburse the eastern feeder for his purchases of western grown grains. This measure is designed to help the eastern farmer, but at the same time it is an incentive to the movement of western grown grains which the western Canadian farmers certainly appreciate.
This session of parliament has granted, almost to the last detail, those things for which the farmers in western Canada have asked. There has been the amendment to the P.F.A.A. to which all who produce grain in western Canada contribute on every bushel they sell. The problem of crop insurance and farm credit has been under study, and the Prime Minister has held out hope that those things will be brought before us at the next session of parliament.
The government must have had a good reason for deciding that farms of 200 acres or less were the ones upon which to base their short term assistance. Some people in western Canada will be disappointed that the government did not decide on a unit that could more properly be described as an average size farm in grain growing areas. I have given this matter a great deal of consideration, and have come to the conclusion that perhaps as a result of this choice the government has allowed a principle to be established upon which farm people will be able to build a powerful case when the ranks are finally closed as between farmers in all parts of Canada, and when they come armed with the statistical data to establish their right to a full and fair share of the national income.
From each of the western provinces there have been those who have devoted themselves diligently and faithfully to their constituents in this matter. It has been a source of satisfaction to be associated with them in the agricultural caucus of our party. I think it is only fitting that on this occasion so near the end of the session I should express the appreciation and satisfaction that has come to us all as members from other parts of Canada
Supply-Agriculture
have shown the same desire and capacity to envision a truly national policy for agriculture.
If I have one regret in this whole matter I hope that I may be pardoned. It is that the constituency of Assiniboia did not have a representative in the government caucus to speak for the people of that great grain growing area of Saskatchewan. Their representative in the commons could only ask the question: "When?" It did not matter how many times he asked that question, it did not add a single dollar to the amount embodied in this estimate. In fact, the hon. member for Assiniboia seems to have forgotten-
